docs.title: Home
docs.text:
PHOS is an open-source, bidirectional physical I/O layer for AI agents, powered by the Model Context Protocol. Your external agent provides reasoning; the local Raspberry Pi runtime provides physical perception and execution.

Bring your own agent. Bring your own hardware. Use a compatible MCP client and the supported Pi peripherals or a controller implementing phos-hw v1. Hardware features depend on the devices and providers configured in your build.

docs.title: Bringing AI agents into the physical world.
docs.text:
Eyes, voice and senses for AI agents.

Give your agent physical context and a way to communicate beyond chat. PHOS connects supported sensors to AI agents and turns authorized requests into expressive eyes, speech, and visual signals.

Connect your agent How PHOS works

docs.text:
Explore two English-language demos from the official PHOS channel: live physical context through MCP and analysis of recent environmental history.

docs.title: Perceive, react, express
docs.text:
• Perceive

    Read available environmental measurements, motion, human presence, and attention as structured physical context, with availability and freshness. Your agent uses PHOS interfaces instead of managing sensor drivers.

    Explore physical awareness

  • React

    Compatible clients subscribe to resource changes and retrieve updated context without continuously polling for semantic transitions. Your agent or host decides whether to respond.

    Understand resource updates

  • Express

    Communicate activity through animated eyes, supported expressions, and a temporary thinking state. Add configured speech or controller-backed LED signals so people can notice agent activity away from a chat window.

    See the interaction model

docs.title: How PHOS works
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    sensors["Physical sensors and controllers"]
    runtime["PHOS runtime and semantic context"]
    resources["MCP resources and update notifications"]
    agent["External MCP client and agent"]
    tools["MCP tools and permission checks"]
    outputs["Eyes, speech and LED signals"]
    sensors -->|Pi adapters or phos-hw v1| runtime
    runtime --> resources --> agent
    agent --> tools --> runtime
    runtime --> outputs

MCP connects agents to PHOS. The separate phos-hw v1 serial protocol connects compatible external controllers to the Pi. The official ESP32 firmware is a reference implementation; an external controller is optional. The local PHOS runtime is required for physical execution.

docs.title: One physical interface, different agents
docs.text:
PHOS works through MCP rather than a particular model or agent framework. Register independent agent identities, issue separate bearer credentials, and choose read-only observer or action-capable standard access. Multiple clients use the same runtime; physical outputs remain shared and subject to PHOS arbitration. PHOS provides no agent orchestration or isolated output devices.

Resource reads and tool calls pass through application permissions and runtime checks. Camera snapshots require separate permission and are requested on demand. Resource notifications contain a URI, not images or sensor payloads; they are best-effort cues rather than a guaranteed event stream.

Explore agent access and security

docs.title: What will you build?
docs.text:
• A physical presence for an agent: express activity or speak a concise reply.
  • Coding feedback you can notice: have your integration request a thinking visual during a task and a supported expression or LED signal on completion.
  • Presence-aware interactions: let external logic read confirmed anonymous presence and decide when a response is useful.
  • Environmental context: let an agent retrieve available measurements or bounded history and explain them to a person.

These are integration ideas using implemented interfaces. The external workflow and its decision logic are yours to build. Explore use cases.

docs.title: Get started
docs.text:
Your goal Start here Connect an external agent to a running PHOS Connect your first MCP client Build the physical interface Build PHOS · Hardware BOM Connect or develop compatible hardware Hardware architecture · Controller protocol Run PHOS locally without an external agent Standalone operation Build integrations and contribute Contribution opportunities

The reference runtime targets Raspberry Pi 3 with a 5-inch 800×600 display. Camera, sensors, voice, and external controllers are optional; setup guides explain each capability's requirements. Personalize the face with skins after setting up your interaction.

docs.title: License audit inventory
docs.text: This is a repository inventory prepared for the Apache-2.0 adoption. It is not legal advice, a complete software bill of materials, or a representation that all dependencies are license-compatible. License texts and obligations must be verified from the exact distribution that a release includes.

docs.title: First-party status
docs.text:
The repository did not document a copyright holder when this audit was made. The root NOTICE therefore uses [COPYRIGHT HOLDER]; a maintainer must confirm the owner and replace that placeholder before publication. Git author names are not by themselves proof of copyright ownership or contribution authority.

Repository-owned Python files under src/robot/ carry an Apache-2.0 SPDX identifier. This does not relicense vendored assets, external model files, or contributions whose authorization has not been established.

docs.title: Repository delivery boundaries
docs.text:
• No package.json, platformio.ini, ESP32 firmware source, or Git submodule was present in this checkout at audit time.
  • The official ESP32 firmware is maintained at phosairobot/phos-esp32; firmware license and dependency review must occur in that source repository.
  • Python dependency ranges are not a release inventory. Before publishing a binary image, wheel, container, or installer, produce a locked inventory for that artifact and preserve required notices.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: The robot must not depend on a single AI vendor or model.

docs.title: Contract
docs.text:
Application code talks to LLMProvider:

  • input: neutral LLMMessage objects
  • optional input: neutral LLMTool definitions
  • output: neutral LLMResponse
  • tool requests: neutral LLMToolCall objects

docs.title: Provider adapters
docs.text:
Initial adapter locations:

  • ai/providers/openai_provider.py
  • ai/providers/anthropic_provider.py
  • ai/providers/local_provider.py

Only these adapters may import vendor SDKs.

docs.title: Normal mode
docs.text: Use a fast, relatively inexpensive remote model for ordinary dialogue and tool selection.

docs.title: Complex mode (future)
docs.text: A routing policy may escalate selected tasks to a stronger model. Routing must target capabilities/configured providers, not hard-code application behavior around a brand.

docs.title: Offline mode (future)
docs.text: A small model may handle limited offline tasks. Raspberry Pi 3 performance constraints mean a LAN-hosted model is also considered a local/offline-capable backend when the local network is available.

docs.title: Speech
docs.text:
Initially keep these stages independent:

microphone -> STT -> RobotAgent/LLMProvider -> TTS -> speaker

This is easier to debug and permits changing each component independently. Realtime end-to-end voice can be evaluated later.

docs.title: Home Assistant tools
docs.text: Home Assistant actions are exposed as robot tools rather than direct model API access. Maintain an allow-list for permitted actions. High-impact actions such as locks, alarms or garage access must not become available merely because a provider supports tool calling.

docs.title: Local REST API
docs.text:
The PHOS local REST contract is OpenAPI 3.1. It is a versioned public contract for /api/v1; all control remains semantic and flows through PhosApplicationService, never directly to hardware. See Remote API for the endpoint guide, authentication behavior, and operational examples.

GET /api/v1/capabilities is operation-oriented. Its commands mapping identifies each writable semantic operation with its endpoint, HTTP method, request field, and allowed values. Its observable_states mapping lists runtime-readable vocabulary, including values such as error that clients must not submit. Both projections are derived from PHOS domain validation rules.

GET /api/v1/overlay separates sensor-derived environmental intent, the manual transient override, and the arbitrated resolved intent currently presented by PHOS. A POST /api/v1/overlay request may set either independent channel (temperature: none/cold/warm; air_quality: none/warning/bad) for an optional positive duration_ms; DELETE clears only that override and immediately returns to current environmental intent.

POST /api/v1/speak accepts {"text":"Hello from PHOS."} and returns 202 {"status":"accepted"} after the main runtime accepts a bounded (500 character) TTS request. It shares the existing authenticated Web Admin session and application-service/IPC boundary; see Remote API.

curl -X GET http://localhost:8080/api/v1/overlay
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/overlay -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"temperature":"warm","duration_ms":3000}'
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/overlay -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"temperature":"cold","air_quality":"warning","duration_ms":5000}'
curl -X DELETE http://localhost:8080/api/v1/overlay

Validate the checked-in contract with:

PYTHONPATH=src python -m robot.web.openapi

The normal local server is deliberately conservative: use the canonical web bind address and port, retain its administrator authentication, and put TLS plus additional authentication at a trusted reverse proxy for any non-local access. The OpenAPI server URL is deliberately relative (/), so Swagger UI always targets the host and port that served /docs; it never assumes port 8080. REST endpoints use the existing phos_admin HttpOnly, SameSite session cookie; there is no API token or second account store. Unauthenticated /api/... requests receive JSON 401 unauthorized, while an authenticated session that must complete its bootstrap password change receives JSON 403 forbidden. Log in at /login first, then open /docs: Swagger UI is same-origin and automatically reuses the browser session cookie. After administrator login, local interactive documentation is available at /docs and the raw contract at /openapi.json. Swagger UI JavaScript and CSS are served from PHOS package assets, so these pages and the contract work offline; ReDoc is intentionally not exposed because no local ReDoc bundle is currently shipped. The events endpoint is Server-Sent Events under the current WSGI deployment; the contract documents that transport explicitly.

docs.title: Repository ownership
docs.text:
• phos — owns the Raspberry Pi runtime, application services, MCP Streamable HTTP server, REST API, Web Admin, Vision and Voice.
  • phos-mcp-bridge — is the Node.js 20+ transport adapter between local MCP stdio and PHOS Streamable HTTP. It reads bearer auth from PHOS_MCP_TOKEN, performs no identity or permission decisions, and never automatically retries tools/call.
  • phos-esp32 — owns the companion phos-hw v1 firmware: ESP32 sensor acquisition and WS2812B physical execution.

docs.title: Remote application boundary
docs.text:
Remote control is mediated by robot.services.PhosApplicationService.

  • REST, Web Admin, event-stream, MCP, and Voice adapters — Use semantic commands and read models from this boundary; they do not access camera, GPIO, I2C sensors, LED providers, or renderer internals.
  • RobotCore / BehaviorEngine — Receive state changes delegated by the service.
  • Lifecycle — Receives configuration work delegated by the service.

The following diagram shows the Core, subsystem, and provider boundaries.

flowchart TD
  core["Robot Core<br/>Lifecycle, state and events"]
  core --> voice[Voice]
  core --> ai["AI interfaces"]
  core --> ui[UI]
  voice --> mic[Microphone] --> speech["STT / TTS"]
  ai --> agent["Agent / tools"] --> llm[LLMProvider] --> adapters[Provider adapters]
  ui --> display["Display / eyes"]
  vision[Vision] -->|Observations and events| core
  hardware[Hardware adapters] -->|Typed observations| core
  style core fill:#2e1065,stroke:#a855f7,color:#fff

docs.title: External Hardware Controller Protocol v1
docs.text: PHOS defines a hardware-agnostic USB/serial controller boundary in robot.hardware.controller_protocol; it is not an ESP32 protocol.

docs.title: Framing and envelope
docs.text:
It uses UTF-8 JSON Lines, one bounded object per newline, with the envelope:

  • protocol: "phos-hw"
  • version: 1
  • type
  • Optional id
  • Optional reply_to
  • Object payload

Controllers push semantic sensor/motion events and advertise capabilities; PHOS does not poll them.

docs.title: Inbound messages and sensor mapping
docs.text:
The v1 source currently specifies the payload only where PHOS consumes it. Strict payload validation applies to:

  • motion_update
  • orientation_update
  • set_led_animation

The serial adapter also maps sensor_update values into existing semantic services:

  • Temperature (c).
  • Pressure (hpa).
  • Humidity (%).
  • eCO2 (ppm).
  • TVOC (ppb).
  • The push proof ({"sensor":"push","event":"pressed"}).

capabilities remains controller-defined metadata; LED output is available only for the active serial session when that metadata advertises LED support. Other recognized v1 event types are retained as diagnostics but have no Raspberry semantic mapping yet.

docs.title: Outbound commands
docs.text:
PHOS currently transmits only:

  • request_capabilities
  • ping
  • Resolved set_led_animation commands.

The remaining accepted command names are reserved protocol vocabulary, not Web or API controls.

Bounded LED animations

  • off
  • solid
  • blink
  • pulse
  • breathe
  • chase
  • spin
  • wipe

breathe accepts color, brightness, period/duration and min/max intensity. Controllers execute timing, but never invent PHOS semantics.

docs.title: Connection and validation boundaries
docs.text: Heartbeats use reconnectable transports; a stale peer is unhealthy. PHOS treats LED output as unavailable for that session; any controller-local LED fallback is firmware-owned. Unknown top-level fields are ignored, while unknown types and versions receive bounded protocol errors. Sensor events must still enter existing semantic services and BehaviorEngine ownership. The Raspberry Pi serial adapter is reconnectable and configured with a manual device path.

docs.title: Directional LED semantics
docs.text:
Directional LED fields are protocol semantics, not physical LED indexes.

  • spin — Is circular and defaults to clockwise; it accepts only clockwise or counterclockwise direction.
  • chase and wipe — Default to circular/clockwise; their circular form accepts clockwise/counterclockwise direction (wipe may also name a top/bottom/left/right origin). Their symmetric form requires an origin plus outward or inward direction.
  • off — Rejects all directional fields.
  • solid — Rejects all directional fields.
  • blink — Rejects all directional fields.
  • pulse — Rejects all directional fields.
  • breathe — Rejects all directional fields.

Top, bottom, left and right are logical positions: each controller implementation owns its physical index mapping and must preserve these v1 defaults for payloads that omit the new optional fields.

docs.title: Touch input mapping
docs.text: For the initial inbound proof, a controller pushes sensor_update with {"sensor":"push","event":"pressed"}. PHOS maps this to its existing completed touch/tap semantic boundary; it does not poll the controller or add controller-specific behavior logic.

docs.title: Controller-backed provider configuration
docs.text:
For controller-backed sensors:

  1. Set hardware_controller.enabled: true.

  2. Set the corresponding canonical provider to controller:

    • sensors.environmental.provider
    • sensors.ens160.provider
    • sensors.imu.provider

  3. Retain enabled: true.

This prevents local I2C workers from starting while controller sensor_update messages update the same semantic snapshots used by the application services. The controller is a generic provider, not a hardware vendor identity. The committed default remains local and does not enable optional controller hardware.

docs.title: IMU message contracts
docs.text:
Controller IMU telemetry uses two validated v1 messages:

motion_update has exactly:

{"state": "stationary|moving|tilt_left|tilt_right|tilt_forward|tilt_backward|shake|impact", "intensity": "low|medium|high"}

Intensity is semantic movement intensity, never linear velocity.

orientation_update has exactly:

  • acceleration_m_s2 — Vector with finite numeric x, y, and z axes in m/s².
  • angular_velocity_dps — Vector with finite numeric x, y, and z axes in degrees/second.

Both update the existing IMU service; semantic motion and telemetry remain independent snapshot fields.

docs.title: Transient semantic overlays
docs.text:
SemanticOverlayService owns bounded, source-scoped presentation requests:

  • success
  • info
  • attention
  • warning
  • error
  • sensor_alert

Each source owns one request; replacement affects only that source. Requests are plain-text (maximum 120 characters), expire on monotonic time, and resolve by priority from highest to lowest as shown below. Equal-priority requests resolve to the newest request.

flowchart LR
  error[error] --> warning[warning] --> sensor[sensor_alert]
  sensor --> attention[attention] --> success[success] --> info[info]
  style error fill:#2e1065,stroke:#a855f7,color:#fff

The renderer receives only an immutable visible intent/message view, never caller-supplied drawing details.

The existing interpreted air-quality warning/bad event is the only automatic v1 sensor source; it requests sensor_alert without inspecting raw providers.

docs.title: Overlay boundaries and display order
docs.text: This system is internal to the application-service boundary in v1: it adds no REST endpoint. It is independent of RobotState, FaceState, environmental markers, and state effects. The compact semantic card renders after camera preview but before the final local administrative layer. Recovery and Admin QR overlays therefore remain secret-bearing system overlays above it, retain their existing touch behavior, and are not dismissible by semantic requests.

docs.title: Semantic Physical Context
docs.text:
The physical-context read model combines canonical semantics through the shared application-service boundary:

flowchart TD
  n0["Sensors / Vision / RobotState"]
  n1["Canonical semantic services"]
  n2["Semantic Physical Context"]
  n3["PhosApplicationService"]
  n4["Agent / MCP / REST adapters"]
  n0 --> n1 --> n2 --> n3 --> n4
  style n0 fill:#2e1065,stroke:#a855f7,color:#fff

SemanticPhysicalContext is a read-only, build-on-read perception model. It combines canonical robot, environmental, air-quality, motion, presence, attention, and observed-expression semantics. Each section preserves its own availability and freshness state, so partial context remains useful. It exposes no provider/device identity, raw camera data, identity, renderer state, LED state, or controller health. It adds no REST endpoint or MCP adapter; /api/v1/status remains the broader operational status contract.

docs.title: Minimal Agent Permission Model
docs.text:
Agent operations pass through permission checks before application services:

flowchart TD
  n0["External agent"]
  n1["Agent permission boundary"]
  n2["PhosApplicationService"]
  n3["Behavior / Voice / Physical Context / Semantic Signals"]
  n0 --> n1 --> n2 --> n3
  style n0 fill:#2e1065,stroke:#a855f7,color:#fff

AgentApplicationService is a small, provider-independent facade for future trusted agent adapters. It checks an immutable AgentAccess set before delegating to the existing PhosApplicationService; it never grants access to providers, renderers, controller transports, or configuration internals. The canonical operation mapping is:

Operation Permission status READ_STATUS get_physical_context READ_PHYSICAL_CONTEXT presence READ_PERCEPTION attention READ_PERCEPTION observed_expression READ_PERCEPTION set_expression CONTROL_EXPRESSION speak CONTROL_VOICE sleep CONTROL_SLEEP wake CONTROL_SLEEP signal_user SIGNAL_USER set_visual_state CONTROL_VISUAL_STATE

docs.title: State transitions and visual leases
docs.text:
Sleep and wake remain normal state transitions; a signal remains subject to existing semantic LED arbitration.

An agent visual-state request is an identity-scoped, expiring presentation lease, not a lifecycle transition: only thinking may be acquired and idle releases the caller's lease. The effective visual state preserves Core priority for error, sleeping, speaking, and listening, and never mutates RobotCore.state.

docs.title: Permission profiles and excluded controls
docs.text: The in-code standard profile contains that explicit complete v1 set; the observer profile contains only the three read permissions. Configured agent identities select a profile through the canonical agent registry. Raw LED animation, renderer internals, continuous camera-frame access, serial/controller transport, hardware/configuration mutation, and administrative/recovery controls are intentionally absent from this facade.

docs.title: Permission, capability, and authentication
docs.text:
• Permission — Answers whether an identity may request an operation.
  • Capability — Answers whether the delegated application service can currently perform it; validation, availability, lifecycle, and arbitration errors still come from that service after a permission check.
  • Authentication — Answers who is calling.

MCP resolves one immutable provider-neutral AgentIdentity per inbound request before constructing the identity-bound facade. Configured bearer credentials select independent agents; with no credential references, the compatibility path selects the configured default identity without credential verification. Authentication modes and the credential lifecycle are documented in the MCP reference. Network access, TLS, OS permissions, and deployment isolation remain separate concerns.

docs.title: MCP Semantic Adapter — Stage 1
docs.text:
The MCP adapter delegates through the existing agent and application boundaries:

flowchart TD
  n0["MCP client"]
  n1["MCP semantic adapter"]
  n2["Agent permission boundary"]
  n3["PhosApplicationService"]
  n4["PHOS runtime / services"]
  n0 --> n1 --> n2 --> n3 --> n4
  style n0 fill:#2e1065,stroke:#a855f7,color:#fff

Stage 1 uses the official Python mcp SDK (the bounded 2.x line) over Streamable HTTP. PHOS owns the listener lifecycle: normal runtime startup creates one listener over the existing application services, and normal runtime shutdown closes it.

docs.title: Request/response tools
docs.text:
It exposes seventeen request/response tools.

Status and physical context

  • phos_get_status
  • phos_get_physical_context
  • phos_get_physical_assessment

Perception and camera

  • phos_get_presence
  • phos_get_attention
  • phos_get_observed_expression
  • phos_get_camera_snapshot
  • phos_capture_camera_snapshot
  • phos_get_visible_objects

Expressions, state, speech, and signals

  • phos_set_expression
  • phos_speak
  • phos_sleep
  • phos_wake
  • phos_signal_user
  • phos_set_state

Retained physical history

  • phos_query_measurements
  • phos_list_physical_transitions

Every one delegates through AgentApplicationService; MCP owns no permissions, runtime state, provider, or hardware logic.

docs.title: Client sessions and deployment boundaries
docs.text:
MCP clients connect to the already-running PHOS instance. Client sessions do not create runtimes, application services, or permission boundaries. The default listener is loopback-only; a non-loopback bind requires explicit configuration and emits a warning. PHOS bearer authentication and operation permissions do not replace network restrictions or TLS deployment policy.

This is for trusted local/integrated execution. Configure credential references for distinct bearer-authenticated agents; the credential-free compatibility path is not transport authentication. Do not expose the endpoint on the public Internet. Raw hardware, controller transport, renderer internals, continuous video, audio-device management, configuration, and administrative/recovery controls are absent. Protected on-demand camera snapshots are available through the semantic facade.

docs.title: Semantic events and resource updates
docs.text:
Stage 2 begins with a transport-neutral semantic event model. The application service projects meaningful interpreted transitions (robot state, environmental and air-quality conditions, motion, presence, attention, and observed expression) into events with stable fields:

  • type
  • timestamp
  • source
  • payload

It does not emit raw telemetry, provider/device details, or confidence jitter.

docs.title: Event filtering and status projection
docs.text: Consumers may request a validated allow-list of stable event types; each subscription defensively suppresses only adjacent identical semantic events during a short internal window, so a real transition from A to B and back to A remain visible. The model is an internal observer boundary—not the Core event bus and not an MCP feature. It projects canonical agent-status availability as one compact capability_changed event per changed capability, and canonical degraded state as system_health_changed. The first ready-status snapshot establishes a baseline and emits neither startup availability nor health events; later comparisons use the same availability/degraded projection as phos_get_status, with health reasons sorted before comparison.

docs.title: Subscription ownership and cleanup
docs.text: Each observer owns an explicit SemanticSubscription handle with an opaque process-local identifier, active state, idempotent close(), and optional context-manager cleanup. The publisher holds the handler strongly only while the handle is active; explicit close is the required ownership boundary. A dispatch snapshot already in progress may complete when a handle is closed, but no later delivery starts after close() returns.

docs.title: MCP notification delivery
docs.text: The MCP adapter may consume this model through its bounded McpSemanticEventBridge: standard MCP subscriptions/listen clients receive URI-only notifications/resources/updated cues and re-read the relevant Resource. This remains separate from the Core event bus; REST/WebSocket delivery and an optional future MCP Events webhook adapter are not Core responsibilities. Camera resources remain excluded from semantic push cues.

docs.title: Agent status projection
docs.text:
phos_get_status is intentionally narrower than /api/v1/status. Its agent status document contains only:

  • running
  • state
  • Semantic subsystem availability.
  • degraded
  • degraded_reasons

It contains no sensor or perception values (those belong to physical context), provider/device/model details, controller session data, LED animation resolution, display state, or administrative diagnostics. The projection is owned by AgentApplicationService, not the MCP adapter, so future trusted agent adapters share the same contract.

docs.title: 1. Separation of concerns
docs.text: Core coordinates lifecycle, state, events and behavior. Subsystems implement capabilities.

docs.title: 2. Hardware abstraction
docs.text: Business logic depends on interfaces, not GPIO/device-specific code. Ordinary unit tests must not require physical hardware.

docs.title: 3. Events where they reduce coupling
docs.text: Use events for meaningful asynchronous state changes such as speech recognition, robot-state changes or stable Vision observations. Do not create an event merely to avoid a normal function call.

docs.title: 4. Explicit robot state
docs.text: The existing state model includes IDLE, LISTENING, THINKING, SPEAKING, SLEEPING and ERROR. Keep transitions explicit and testable.

docs.title: 5. Incremental verification
docs.text: PHOS is developed through runnable vertical milestones. Existing code may be ahead of the current verified milestone, but new work should prove one capability before expanding the next major subsystem.

docs.title: Visual / behavior path
docs.text:
The visual path separates observation, behavior, rendering, and display composition:

flowchart TD
  camera[Camera] --> vision[Vision] --> events[Stable observations and events]
  events --> core[Robot Core] --> behavior[BehaviorEngine] --> face[FaceState]
  face --> renderer[EyeRenderer] --> display[EyeDisplay composition]
  vision --> preview[Latest preview snapshot] --> runtime[PhosRuntime] --> display
  style behavior fill:#2e1065,stroke:#a855f7,color:#fff
  • Vision — Observes.
  • Behavior — Interprets observations in the context of PHOS's own RobotState.
  • EyeRenderer — Consumes only FaceState and handles rendering/animation details.
  • Display adapter — May compose an optional local diagnostic preview from a UI-neutral snapshot supplied by PhosRuntime; it never accesses camera or Vision providers.

The face-rendering frequency is independent from Vision timing so the display can remain smooth while detection/inference runs at a lower rate.

BehaviorEngine currently lives under src/robot/core/, because behavior is part of Core orchestration in the checked-out implementation.

docs.title: Visual reaction semantics
docs.text:
Vision classifies an uncertain visible facial expression, not a person's internal emotional state. BehaviorEngine gives PHOS its own response and produces the UI-neutral FaceState; Vision never selects renderer geometry or colors directly.

Stable visible-expression observation PHOS behavior FaceExpression VisualAccent neutral calm acknowledgement neutral neutral happiness / happy warm, friendly response happy warm surprise / surprised alert, open response surprised alert unknown (including rejected/negative FER classes) preserve and decay to baseline unchanged, then neutral unchanged, then neutral

Vision publishes semantic evidence, not individual negative FER labels. UNKNOWN is an explicit absence of accepted evidence. It is distinct from a positively confirmed neutral observation; current uncalibrated models abstain on neutral. See docs/vision.md for thresholds and temporal rules.

docs.title: Face intent and renderer mapping
docs.text:
FaceState carries these independently:

  • Expression.
  • Semantic VisualAccent.
  • reaction_strength.

Its optional signed eye_asymmetry is provider-neutral visual intent:

  • Positive — Opens the left eye by that amount and closes the right by the same amount.
  • Negative — Mirrors it.
  • Zero — Requests equal eyes.
  • Absent — The renderer uses the expression profile's ordinary shape.

The renderer maps accents to its own color palette:

Accent Color Neutral Light cyan/white Warm Turquoise Curious Cyan/blue Alert Amber Sleepy Muted violet Error Red

Strength blends the neutral and accent colors, as well as the existing eye-shape profile.

Eye, pupil, and background color transitions interpolate at render cadence rather than jumping at Vision inference cadence.

docs.title: Environmental overlays
docs.text: Environmental interpretation also supplies independent, confirmed temperature and air-quality overlay intents on FaceState. They are composable renderer inputs only: the single priority-selected EnvironmentalState remains the contract for existing eye and LED behavior, while the display can show, for example, both a warm-temperature marker and an air-quality haze without reinterpreting sensor readings or thresholds.

docs.title: Robot-state priority and reaction timing
docs.text:
Robot state remains higher priority than Vision:

  • Listening/thinking — Use a curious accent.
  • Speaking — Uses warm.
  • Sleeping — Uses sleepy.
  • Error — Uses red.

Expression reaction timing

  • Happy reactions — Refresh only from confirmed observations and decay smoothly back to neutral when evidence stops.

  • Surprise — Is temporary, cannot refresh from a sustained pose, and needs confirmed alternative evidence plus a cooldown to rearm.

  • UNKNOWN — Allows normal decay.

  • Face tracking and blink timing — Remain independent from expression inference.

VisualAccent is provider-neutral visual intent for the face. The WS2812B ring in the PHOS hardware build connects to the ESP32; its output uses the semantic controller path below rather than a per-pixel renderer feed.

flowchart LR
  behavior[BehaviorEngine] --> face[FaceState] --> eyes[EyeRenderer] --> display[Display]
  intent[Robot state / environment / user signal] --> arbiter[SemanticLedService]
  arbiter --> controller[ControllerService]
  controller -->|phos-hw v1 serial JSONL| esp[ESP32 controller]
  esp --> ring[WS2812B ring]
  style arbiter fill:#2e1065,stroke:#a855f7,color:#fff
  style esp fill:#1e293b,stroke:#8b5cf6,color:#fff

docs.title: External-controller semantic LED arbitration
docs.text:
External controller LEDs use a separate semantic path: SemanticLedService owns source-scoped requests, priority arbitration, expiry, and command deduplication; the controller executes only the resolved realtime animation. The intent sources are:

  • RobotState — Contributes one persistent intent.
  • Environmental context — Contributes a lower-priority ambient intent.

  • signal_user — Contributes the bounded semantic signals:

    • success
    • warning
    • error
    • attention

docs.title: Transient signals and persistent errors
docs.text: All user signals, including signal_user("error"), are transient. In contrast, RobotState.ERROR contributes the persistent robot_state/error intent until the robot state changes. Error wins over warning, transient user signals, robot-state intents, and ambient context.

docs.title: Animation ownership and capability changes
docs.text:
Neither BehaviorEngine, Web/API adapters, nor firmware choose animation parameters. On a controller capability report the arbiter reapplies its current winner; when LED capability is absent it retains logical intent and emits no hardware command.

flowchart LR
  n0["RobotState / environment / signal_user"]
  n1["SemanticLedService"]
  n2["ControllerService"]
  n3["ESP32 controller LED executor"]
  n4["WS2812B ring"]
  n0 --> n1 --> n2 --> n3 --> n4
  style n0 fill:#2e1065,stroke:#a855f7,color:#fff

docs.title: Runtime
docs.text:
PhosRuntime is the current application coordinator. It supervises Core/UI and optional Vision tasks and handles lifecycle/failure boundaries.

Keep orchestration thin. Do not move expression classification, rendering geometry or model-provider logic into the runtime. Camera/inference/render/audio work must not collapse into a single blocking loop.

The existence of the integrated runtime does not override milestone discipline: each capability still needs independent runnable verification.

docs.title: AI provider architecture
docs.text:
Model access stays behind the provider-neutral interface:

flowchart TD
  agent["RobotAgent / behaviors / tools"] --> llm[LLMProvider]
  llm --> openai[OpenAI adapter]
  llm --> anthropic[Anthropic adapter]
  llm --> local[Local / LAN adapter]
  style llm fill:#2e1065,stroke:#a855f7,color:#fff
  • LLMProvider — Is the only model interface visible to the rest of the robot.
  • Provider adapters — Translate neutral messages/tools/tool calls to and from vendor-specific formats.

The primary conversational model is not assumed to run on Raspberry Pi 3. Cloud API or LAN-hosted models are valid; a deliberately small local fallback may be explored later.

docs.title: Voice architecture
docs.text:
The voice path separates capture, transcription, intent resolution, authorization, and application execution:

flowchart TD
  n0["USB microphone"]
  n1["AudioCaptureProvider<br/>Native device rate"]
  n2["ResamplingAudioCaptureProvider"]
  n3["PCM16 mono, 16 kHz"]
  n4["VAD"]
  n5["Bounded pre-roll"]
  n6["VoiceCaptureSession"]
  n7["STTProvider"]
  n8["TranscriptResult"]
  n9["InteractionInput"]
  n10["IntentResolver"]
  n11["ResolvedIntent or UnresolvedIntent"]
  n12["CommandRouter"]
  n13["Semantic command route"]
  n14["Explicit source-aware authorization"]
  n15["CommandExecutor"]
  n16["PhosApplicationService"]
  n17["InteractionOutcome"]
  n18["InteractionResponseRenderer"]
  n19["InteractionResponse"]
  n0 --> n1 --> n2 --> n3 --> n4 --> n5 --> n6 --> n7 --> n8 --> n9 --> n10 --> n11 --> n12 --> n13 --> n14 --> n15 --> n16 --> n17 --> n18 --> n19
  style n0 fill:#2e1065,stroke:#a855f7,color:#fff

docs.title: Capture and processing rates
docs.text:
Capture rate and processing rate are deliberately separate. Raspberry Pi 3 validation uses a USB microphone at 44.1 kHz, followed by the one canonical resampling boundary to the 16 kHz stream consumed by VAD and STT; microphones need not support 16 kHz natively.

The current explicit capture session stops at transcription:

stateDiagram-v2
  IDLE --> LISTENING
  LISTENING --> THINKING
  THINKING --> IDLE

docs.title: VAD baseline and pre-roll
docs.text:
VAD confirmation takes time, so its bounded 300 ms pre-roll preserves audio preceding speech-start confirmation. The validated baseline is:

Parameter Baseline value Threshold 50 Speech start 120 ms Silence end 700 ms Minimum utterance 300 ms Maximum utterance 12000 ms Pre-roll 300 ms

These are validated baseline values, not universal calibration values.

docs.title: Transcription providers
docs.text: STTProvider keeps transcription provider-neutral; VoskSTTProvider is the first local/offline implementation, not PHOS's architectural identity. The small English Vosk model validates the local architecture but can have limited accuracy for longer phrases and non-native English accents.

docs.title: Intent resolution, routing, and execution
docs.text:
Voice input publishes status/events and uses centralized runtime state transitions. It does not control GPIO, renderers, LEDs, or BehaviorEngine.

  • robot.interaction — Provides plain TranscriptResult, InteractionInput, and canonical resolved/unresolved intent contracts.

  • Async IntentResolver — Its boundary interprets language only; it has no runtime/hardware access and does not route or execute commands.

  • Selectable deterministic resolver — Has a small exact English/Italian catalog for state, expression, temperature, pressure, and air-quality commands; see Voice Commands for the user-facing accepted phrases.

  • Main runtime — When interaction is enabled, observes completed voice transcripts and publishes resolution events/status.

  • CommandRouter — Separately validates a resolved canonical intent and maps it to a semantic command.

  • Voice execution — Is opt-in through interaction.execution_enabled (false by default): the coordinator creates a voice-scoped allowlist, then CommandExecutor invokes sleep, wake, expression, and authorized sensor commands through PhosApplicationService.

docs.title: Query outcomes and spoken responses
docs.text:
Sensor queries reuse that service's read models and produce an InteractionOutcome with canonical numeric fields; unavailable snapshots are normal outcomes.

The pure local InteractionResponseRenderer produces deterministic English or Italian user-facing text from query outcomes.

With interaction.response_tts_enabled (false by default), query responses pass through the application speech boundary and the existing synthesis/playback path:

flowchart LR
  synthesis[TTSProvider] --> playback[AudioOutputProvider]
  style synthesis fill:#2e1065,stroke:#a855f7,color:#fff

This includes SPEAKING; actions and unresolved input remain silent.

The current provider-neutral TTS contract accepts text only, so response language is retained as interaction metadata rather than passed as a provider-specific argument.

TTS adapters are implemented for:

  • Local Piper.
  • Cartesia.
  • ElevenLabs.

Phrase resolution, command routing/execution, wake words, continuous listening, LLM conversation, and Home Assistant remain future work.

docs.title: Physical voice validation
docs.text: Physical validation on Raspberry Pi 3 with a USB microphone confirmed native capture, resampling from 44.1 kHz to 16 kHz, VAD, preserved speech onset through pre-roll, local Vosk transcription, and return to IDLE.

docs.title: Vision architecture
docs.text:
Vision keeps capture, detection, expression classification, and smoothing separate:

flowchart TD
  n0["Picamera2CameraProvider"]
  n1["FaceDetector"]
  n2["ExpressionProvider"]
  n3["ExpressionSmoother"]
  n4["Provider-neutral Vision result / event"]
  n0 --> n1 --> n2 --> n3 --> n4
  style n0 fill:#2e1065,stroke:#a855f7,color:#fff

Use lightweight processing appropriate for Raspberry Pi 3. Expression classification describes uncertain visible facial-expression patterns, not a person's true mental/emotional state. No identity recognition or frame persistence by default.

docs.title: Home Assistant relationship
docs.text: Home Assistant is an integration/tool surface, not PHOS's brain. Commands may use REST, state/events may use WebSocket, and MQTT may later expose PHOS entities. AI access must be mediated by explicit tools/services and allowlists; sensitive actions require explicit policy.

docs.title: Local/cloud expression boundary
docs.text:
Local and optional cloud providers share the expression-smoothing and behavior path:

flowchart LR
  camera[Camera] --> crop[Local detector / selector / square crop]
  crop --> provider[ExpressionProvider]
  provider --> local[OpenCVExpressionProvider]
  provider --> cloud[Optional AWSExpressionProvider]
  local --> smoother[ExpressionSmoother]
  cloud --> smoother
  smoother --> events[Vision events] --> behavior[BehaviorEngine] --> face[FaceState]
  style provider fill:#2e1065,stroke:#a855f7,color:#fff

docs.title: Provider execution and observation provenance
docs.text: AWS SDK objects remain in its adapter. Cloud requests use a single background asyncio task plus to_thread, independent of capture/tracking/render cadence. Provider lifecycle invalidation discards evidence across tracking discontinuity. Cached ExpressionObservation.sampled_at preserves provenance so reads cannot manufacture temporal confirmation. Local observations retain their existing cadence and semantics. See Vision.

docs.title: Canonical configuration and secrets
docs.text:
config/phos.yaml is the sole supported source of normal runtime settings.

  • The provider-neutral robot.config module validates its required sections and maps them to RuntimeConfig and CloudExpressionConfig, with no hardware, SDK or argparse dependencies.

  • The runtime passes only relevant typed values to each subsystem.

  • Startup validates before constructing any camera/display components; paths are relative to the configuration file.

  • Existing constructor fallback values are not consulted by application composition.

The same file/dict validation, serialization and atomic persistence must be used by the optional web configuration interface. Credentials are never fields in application settings.

SecretsService keeps runtime-only provider credentials in an authenticated encrypted local store; its web facade reports slot status and permits replacement/removal but deliberately cannot read values.

New ordinary settings must extend this central model/file, not standalone CLI arguments.

Existing CLI settings are deprecated explicit overrides during migration.

docs.title: Reload, live activation, and restart
docs.text:
• Reload through the lifecycle service — Logging level, display iris appearance, and camera-preview settings.
  • Runtime-aware live activation and persistence — Supported Voice & Speech STT/TTS/audio changes.
  • Restart — Other subsystem changes require restart. See configuration reference.

docs.title: Administration adapter
docs.text:
robot.web wraps the canonical configuration service with structured settings forms and an advanced YAML editor, both backed by the same ConfigRepository.

  • Credentials page — Uses the write-only WebSecretsService facade, never SecretsService.get_secret, so secrets cannot enter page rendering or an administrative response.

Provider integration remains separate from this storage foundation.

docs.title: Web worker and authentication boundaries
docs.text:
Waitress runs in a separate process owned by the main startup lifecycle, independent of rendering/Vision. It receives startup settings for a saved-versus-startup comparison; runtime-backed pages request semantic status through the bounded application/lifecycle channel rather than reading subsystem internals directly.

Its password-storage service is separate from runtime JSON; Flask sessions and Flask-WTF protect administration actions. Core, providers and the renderer have no web-framework dependency. See the web manual.

docs.title: Settings domains and persistence
docs.text: Administration domains select canonical field paths for presentation only. Each page merges its submitted fields into the complete document and calls the same validation/persistence boundary. System / Status is read-only; password changes use the separate credential service. See the manual for the domain-to-field map.

docs.title: Shared application services for control surfaces
docs.text:
Web, future remote API, MCP and Voice are adapters around PHOS application services. They reuse the same validation, authorization, configuration and behavior-command services; they must not reach into GPIO, hardware adapters, provider objects, renderer state or other subsystem internals. Add an application service when an approved capability needs one, rather than duplicating behavior in each surface.

The configuration, Remote API, supported Voice & Speech, and MCP semantic application services are implemented examples.

docs.title: Application lifecycle boundary
docs.text:
robot.lifecycle.LifecycleService owns the active-configuration snapshot and allowed operations:

  • Status — Allowed status operation.
  • Reload — Validates the full canonical file before applying logging level, iris appearance, and camera preview through their application-service boundaries.
  • Restart — Allowed restart operation.

Supported Voice & Speech changes use a separate candidate-activation/persistence transaction; other changes remain pending.

The parent process serves a bounded local process channel to the web worker; adapters cannot submit shell commands, paths or arbitrary configuration payloads. Future API/MCP surfaces must use the same policy service.

docs.title: Restart ownership and failure recovery
docs.text:
The supplied user systemd service owns process replacement. A confirmed restart follows this sequence:

  1. Request graceful runtime shutdown and exit code 75.
  2. systemd restarts the same entry point.

The web adapter neither runs OS commands nor spawns replacements. Runtime subsystem and web-worker failures propagate as nonzero process exits for systemd recovery.

docs.title: Preview reload and runtime status
docs.text: Preview reload is acknowledged after camera start/stop acceptance; failed starts release partially acquired camera resources, and shutdown drains preview tasks and supervisor waiters. Manual launches reject browser restart. OS reboot and general remote control remain out of scope. See installation for display-session environment and service permissions. Status distinguishes configured values from runtime active/availability state where that snapshot is available; it does not invent a health-monitoring layer.

docs.title: Eye appearance
docs.text:
The dedicated Skin Architecture explains catalog loading, active-agent selection, and the shared appearance lifecycle. See the Skins reference for supported presentation fields.

  • Display & Appearance configuration — Supplies the validated canonical iris color to EyeRenderer at startup.
  • EyeRenderer — Still consumes only FaceState and renderer style configuration; expression/provider labels never reach the renderer.
  • Semantic visual accents — Continue to pass through BehaviorEngine and FaceState.
  • Tk — Draws layered eye-body, iris, pupil and highlight primitives without a raster-processing pipeline.
  • Live iris appearance — Can be applied through the configuration lifecycle and render-loop queue; display geometry/backend changes still require PHOS restart.

docs.title: Environmental sensor service
docs.text:
The separately approved BME280/BMP280 addition follows:

flowchart TD
  n0["BME280 / BMP280"]
  n1["Selected hardware provider"]
  n2["EnvironmentalSensorService"]
  n3["PhosRuntime.sensor_status"]
  n4["LifecycleService status snapshot"]
  n5["Existing local process channel"]
  n6["Authenticated Web Admin Sensors"]
  n0 --> n1 --> n2 --> n3 --> n4 --> n5 --> n6
  style n0 fill:#2e1065,stroke:#a855f7,color:#fff

  • robot.sensors — Owns the provider-neutral contract, immutable measurements and latest-state service.

  • robot.hardware adapters — Alone know the SMBus/driver APIs.

  • hardware.environmental.environmental_provider_type — Centralizes selection and capabilities.

docs.title: Measurement contracts and interpretation
docs.text:
Both return EnvironmentalReading with temperature/pressure and nullable humidity_percent; BMP280 must return null, BME280 must supply humidity. The service validates that invariant using declared available measurements.

The runtime constructs and starts/stops the service and passes only its typed, fresh snapshots to EnvironmentalInterpreter.

The interpreter publishes confirmed semantic state and independent overlay intents to BehaviorEngine; raw readings never reach EyeRenderer, LEDRingController or Vision.

Future compatible environmental providers reuse this boundary; other kinds of sensors need their own typed measurements rather than forcing them into temperature/humidity/pressure fields.

docs.title: Worker lifecycle and freshness
docs.text:
One daemon worker serializes all provider calls; disabled means no worker, provider construction, vendor imports or I2C open. It retries initialization after failures, retains no history and exposes only finite valid current measurements.

Snapshot metadata includes:

  • Active sensor type.
  • Available measurements.
  • Availability/status.
  • UTC last success.
  • Monotonic age.
  • Sanitized error type.

Failed or stale snapshots contain no current values.

A blocked native call cannot stop the render loop or grow a work queue; stop signals the worker and awaits at most one second.

The owner closes the bus when I/O returns; process exit releases it if stuck. No concurrent bus close is used.

docs.title: Configuration and administration access
docs.text:
All settings are restart-only under existing lifecycle classification. Save and Reload do not restart any subsystem. Only an explicitly requested PHOS restart reinitializes hardware.

The Sensors page reads in-memory state via shared services, never imports a driver or infers availability from saved enabled/address values. The existing authenticated process channel carries the snapshot; no new API or IPC operation is exposed. See ADR-022, hardware and configuration migration.

docs.title: Controller-backed ENS160 and AHT21
docs.text:
Controller telemetry enters the shared status and interpretation services:

flowchart LR
  esp[ESP32 telemetry] --> controller[ControllerService]
  controller --> callbacks[Runtime lifecycle callbacks] --> air[AirQualitySensorService]
  air --> status[Runtime / application status] --> clients[WebUI / MCP]
  style air fill:#2e1065,stroke:#a855f7,color:#fff

The controller acquires measurements and publishes phos-hw v1 records; Pi services own freshness, validity, controller-generation isolation and environmental interpretation. ENS160 provides estimated eCO2, TVOC and AQI-UBA; AHT21 temperature and humidity are independently fresh. Retiring a session immediately makes controller readings unusable until fresh telemetry arrives.

docs.title: MPU-6050 IMU extension
docs.text:
The IMU provider feeds the existing sensor-service and runtime status boundary:

flowchart LR
  provider[hardware.MPU6050Provider] --> service[IMUSensorService]
  service --> status[PhosRuntime.sensor_status]
  style service fill:#2e1065,stroke:#a855f7,color:#fff

This path uses the same worker, freshness, retry and authenticated status boundary as the other sensors.

  • IMUReading holds acceleration X/Y/Z in m/s² and angular velocity X/Y/Z in °/s.

  • The hardware adapter alone knows MPU-6050 registers and smbus2; Web Admin only reads snapshots and edits canonical sensors.imu settings.

  • No BehaviorEngine, EyeRenderer or Vision component receives IMU readings.

The adapter applies fixed ±2 g / ±250 °/s scale factors only; offset calibration, fusion and orientation are outside this capability.

docs.title: Motion interpretation extension
docs.text:
Motion interpretation converts readings into provider-neutral semantic observations:

flowchart LR
  reading[IMUReading] --> interpreter[MotionInterpreter] --> motion[MotionState / MotionEvent]
  style interpreter fill:#2e1065,stroke:#a855f7,color:#fff

Motion interpretation is a pure, provider-neutral layer between IMU state and its semantic consumers. It never accesses the MPU-6050, GPIO, Web handlers, Vision, EyeRenderer or BehaviorEngine. The IMU worker supplies timestamped samples and exposes only the current interpreted state and last event through the existing status boundary. STILL, MOVING, four tilt directions, SHAKE and IMPACT are semantic observations consumed by BehaviorEngine through the event bus.

Motion settings reload into the interpreter without reopening the I2C provider.

docs.title: IMU visual behavior extension
docs.text: The IMU service publishes stable semantic state changes to Core's local event bus. BehaviorEngine consumes them and overlays visual intent onto FaceState; the renderer still receives no IMU object or event.

docs.title: Motion-specific visual intent
docs.text:
In IDLE:

  • MOVING — Recenters the pupils, opens the eyes to 1.16 and gives it 0.63 reaction strength.

Tilt reactions move pupils in the corresponding visual direction at 86% of the normalized safe range. All have 0.56 strength and the curious accent.

Tilt Eye opening and asymmetry Horizontal Opening 1.12; mirrored 0.18 signed eye asymmetry. Left tilt opens the left eye and closes the right; right tilt reverses it. Forward Equal eyes, opening to 1.23. Back Equal eyes, closing to 0.82.
  • SHAKE — Is a 1.18-open, 0.88-strength surprised alert.
  • IMPACT — Is the stronger 1.25-open, 1.0-strength alert.

Both hold for 55% of their configured duration then decay smoothly.

docs.title: State priority and resumption
docs.text: ERROR, SLEEPING, LISTENING, THINKING and SPEAKING override IMU intent; motion then resumes only when Core returns to IDLE. Motion overlays take priority over lower-priority Vision expression reactions in IDLE, without changing the user-selected iris theme.

docs.title: Local Admin Access
docs.text:
NetworkInfoService is parent-process runtime state, not configuration: it selects the first non-loopback, non-link-local IPv4 address and refreshes its bounded cached result every 30 seconds.

Web Admin obtains that read model only through RemoteApplicationService and lifecycle.

docs.title: Physical Admin overlay
docs.text: The physical Admin overlay is a separate top display layer. It receives only the effective LAN Admin URL and a cached qrcode matrix; Tk renders individual square canvas modules, so Pillow and image resampling are unnecessary. A top-right double-tap 20% of the display opens it, and a tap closes it. This never changes FaceState, RobotState, or BehaviorEngine state.

docs.title: Build PHOS
docs.text: PHOS is a progressive Raspberry Pi project: begin with the display and add hardware only when the preceding layer works. Follow the setup and wiring instructions for each added capability.

docs.title: Prepare
docs.text:
The documented reference target is a Raspberry Pi 3 running Raspberry Pi OS with a graphical desktop, Python 3.11+, and a 5-inch 800×600 display. Raspberry Pi 4 and 5 compatibility is not established by the repository, so they are not listed as supported replacements. Raspberry Pi OS Lite alone is insufficient for the graphical eye renderer.

Component Status Why it is needed Raspberry Pi 3 Required baseline Runs PHOS. 5-inch 800×600 display Required baseline Shows the face and eyes. Network connection Recommended Clone/install, updates, and optional Web Admin or MCP access. Camera Optional Enables face, presence, attention, snapshots, and optional object awareness. USB microphone and audio output Optional Enables configured voice capture and speech playback. BME280/BMP280, MPU-6050 Optional Adds Pi I²C environmental or motion observations. ESP32 with ENS160/AHT21 Optional Adds controller-backed air-quality and temperature/humidity telemetry. WS2812B ring Optional Connects to the ESP32 for phos-hw v1 semantic LED feedback.

Plan your parts with the Hardware BOM. Exact wiring, voltage limits, and I²C addresses are maintained in the hardware reference. Choose an enclosure and mounts to fit your selected display and modules.

docs.title: Assemble and install
docs.text:
1. Connect the display and confirm that Raspberry Pi OS has an active local graphical desktop.
  2. Follow the canonical installation procedure exactly. It contains the supported package, display, camera, service, and security steps.
  3. Start with the supplied complete config/phos.yaml. It safely enables eyes only; YAML is the only supported runtime configuration format.
  4. Run the documented foreground command before enabling the managed service.
  5. Add one optional capability at a time and perform its linked physical check.

docs.title: First boot checklist
docs.text:
• PHOS starts without a configuration-validation error.
  • The local display shows the animated eyes.
  • The startup output identifies the configuration file you edited.
  • If enabled, Web Admin is reachable only on your trusted LAN and its bootstrap password is changed at first access.
  • Optional camera, controller, sensor, and audio status are checked separately; an unavailable optional device must not be assumed healthy because eyes run.

See installation for commands and troubleshooting, and Web Admin for safe configuration changes.

docs.title: 1. See an expression
docs.text: Requires: the display baseline. Expected result: a supported expression appears through the normal PHOS visual system. Use the Web Admin Controls page or the documented Remote API expression endpoint, rather than trying to access a renderer directly.

docs.title: 2. Read the environment
docs.text: Requires: a configured, available supported sensor. Expected result: Web Admin or the semantic API reports measurement availability and freshness. BMP280 intentionally has no humidity value; ENS160 eCO2 is an estimate, not a direct CO2 measurement. See environmental awareness.

docs.title: 3. Request a semantic signal
docs.text: Requires: a running PHOS instance; an LED ring is optional. Expected result: PHOS accepts a semantic signal through the Remote API or a permitted MCP request. Hardware output is resolved by PHOS and may be unavailable when no LED controller is installed.

docs.title: 4. Connect an Agent
docs.text: Requires: MCP enabled and a compatible client. Expected result: the client reads status or physical context, then performs only an action authorized for its profile. Continue with the developer quickstart.

docs.title: JSON to YAML configuration migration
docs.text:
PHOS uses YAML as its only supported runtime configuration format. Normal PHOS startup never reads, converts, or overwrites a JSON configuration file.

For an older installation that still has phos.json, stop PHOS and run the explicit one-time migration from the checkout:

PYTHONPATH=src .venv/bin/python tools/migrate_phos_json_to_yaml.py \
  config/phos.json config/phos.yaml

The destination must not already exist. The tool validates the complete source document through RuntimeConfig, preserves configuration-relative paths at the new YAML location, writes atomically, and leaves the original JSON source in place as the backup. Correct any reported validation error before starting PHOS with the new YAML file:

PYTHONPATH=src .venv/bin/python -m robot.main --config config/phos.yaml

JSON remains in PHOS API, MCP, and phos-hw JSON Lines protocol contracts; this migration applies only to the runtime configuration file.

docs.title: Contributing and project status
docs.text: PHOS welcomes issue reports, documentation improvements, hardware evidence, and code contributions. The repository contribution process is in the root CONTRIBUTING.md, and PHOS is licensed under the Apache License, Version 2.0.

docs.title: Report or discuss work
docs.text:
• Use the GitHub issue tracker to report reproducible defects or propose a bounded improvement.
  • Include PHOS version, Raspberry Pi/OS details, configuration with secrets removed, exact steps, logs with credentials removed, and the observed result.
  • Do not post bearer credentials, Web Admin passwords, cloud credentials, raw camera frames, or audio in an issue.

docs.title: Before opening a change
docs.text: Read the architecture, accepted decisions, and repository AGENTS.md. Keep hardware-specific details behind existing interfaces, retain hardware-free tests, and record hardware test results with wiring and configuration details.

docs.title: Project maturity
docs.text: The roadmap records planned and unverified work; the release records record milestone scope. Describe optional hardware and external integrations with their configuration requirements and test results.

docs.title: Build on PHOS
docs.text:
• External agent experiences: demonstrate how an agent reads physical context, chooses an action, and uses expressions, thinking visuals, or configured speech.
  • MCP client integrations: show discovery, permission failures, resource reads, subscriptions/listen, reconnection, and explicit decisions before output calls.
  • Hardware controllers: implement the existing phos-hw v1 boundary on new hardware, with capability discovery and the accepted observation mappings. Document a board as supported only with implementation and hardware evidence.
  • Sensors and providers: extend existing adapters and shared semantic services; explain units, freshness, failure behavior, and controller provenance.
  • Physical communication and accessibility: improve expression clarity, reduced-motion experiences, documentation, or interaction examples using the existing visual and application-service boundaries.
  • Community demonstrations: share reproducible configurations, hardware reports, or videos that show what an integration actually does.

Start with use cases, MCP integration, the controller protocol, and skin authoring. Propose changes to public contracts or architecture through the contribution process before implementing them.

docs.title: PHOS Current State
docs.text: This file is an implementation handoff for coding agents. It records what is present in the checked-out repository and distinguishes implementation from hardware verification.

docs.title: Identity and baseline
docs.text:
• Project: PHOS.
  • Python namespace: robot.
  • Target: Raspberry Pi 3.
  • Display target: 5-inch 800x600.
  • Microphone available; exact interface remains TBD.
  • Display/eyes and Pi Camera/tracking are documented as operational in docs/hardware.md; exact camera model remains unspecified.

docs.title: Official companion ESP32 firmware
docs.text: The companion firmware repository is live at phosairobot/phos-esp32. It implements the phos-hw v1 serial JSONL connection for ENS160 + AHT21 telemetry and WS2812B semantic LED control. Makers should follow that repository's build/flashing instructions, then use the PHOS controller setup to enable the Pi-side serial connection and check advertised capabilities.

docs.title: Current source version
docs.text: robot.__version__ and the release test report robot.__version__.

docs.title: Transient Overlay System v1
docs.text: The source implements source-scoped, bounded semantic transient overlays with renderer and protected-admin-layer integration. Automated core and UI coverage passes; physical Raspberry display validation is deferred.

docs.title: Temporal History v0.1
docs.text:
PHOS retains a RAM-only, six-hour rolling history of accepted environmental and air-quality measurements (at most one per metric per minute) and confirmed semantic physical transitions. History is discarded on restart, contains no camera frames, audio, transcripts, or identity, and is exposed only through the read_physical_history permission via phos_query_measurements and phos_list_physical_transitions. It is bounded to 360 samples per metric and 500 transitions; it neither pushes a notification for every sample nor interpolates missing observations.

The repository implements a read-only, provider-independent semantic perception context through PhosApplicationService; it is automated-tested and available to the MCP semantic adapter.

docs.title: Minimal Agent Permission Model
docs.text: The repository implements an in-code, immutable semantic permission boundary for future trusted external-agent adapters. AgentApplicationService delegates only approved semantic reads and actions to PhosApplicationService; it adds no MCP transport, user/account model, persistence, or raw hardware/render surface. standard and read-only observer profiles are automated-tested. This is not a network or OS security boundary; Stage 3.1 adds the separate transitional identity/authentication boundary below.

docs.title: MCP Semantic Adapter — Stage 2
docs.text:
The repository implements a trusted-local Streamable HTTP MCP adapter over AgentApplicationService, with standard semantic read/action tools and read-only semantic snapshot resources (phos://status, phos://physical-context, phos://environment, and the on-demand image/jpeg camera resource phos://vision/snapshot). It runs embedded in the one PHOS runtime owner started by normal PHOS startup; it exposes the configured Streamable HTTP listener over that existing runtime. The camera snapshot is synchronous, read-only and non-streaming; it travels through the application/agent permission boundary without opening another camera. The standard profile has the dedicated read_camera_snapshot permission; the observer profile does not. The stdio phos-mcp-bridge dynamically forwards Resources without snapshot-specific bridge code. Automated coverage verifies preview independence, and Raspberry Pi validation confirmed that phos://vision/snapshot remains available with Camera Preview disabled and returns a non-empty image/jpeg blob. This establishes resource availability and JPEG output, not image-content quality. Async semantic change cues use SDK subscriptions/listen; clients receive URI-only notifications and re-read current Resources. Camera snapshots are excluded from notifications. MCP Stage 3.3 is complete: configured bearer secret_ref values resolve only through SecretsService; valid credentials resolve a request-scoped AgentIdentity and existing permission profile. Missing, malformed, or invalid bearers fail before application execution with no default-agent fallback.

Stage 3.2 loads the canonical agents registry at startup. A configured default agent resolves to AgentIdentity, its existing permission profile, and then the agent application facade. Changes are restart-only. Stage 3.3 adds only non-secret credential references, not tokens, Web Admin management, bridge credentials, or credential-management UI.

MCP Stage 3.4 supplies AgentCredentialService for creation, rotation, revocation, and non-secret status of configured bearer references. It uses the existing encrypted SecretsService; bearer values are generated with the OS CSPRNG, disclosed only at create/rotate time, and are never readable through the lifecycle service. Rotation preserves secret_ref and invalidates the old bearer; revocation removes the stored value while retaining the configured identity/profile. Stage 3.4 itself did not add Web Admin management, bridge transport support, expiry policy, or an external identity provider.

MCP Stage 3.5 adds the authenticated Web Admin Settings → Agents page for existing configured agents. It displays only identity/profile and non-secret credential status, calls AgentCredentialService rather than SecretsService, requires confirmation for rotate/revoke, and renders a newly issued bearer only in its immediate create/rotate response. Agent-definition editing remains the canonical restart-required configuration workflow.

MCP Stage 3.6 is complete in the separately owned phos-mcp-bridge: its stdio transport reads PHOS_MCP_TOKEN and creates an authenticated Streamable HTTP connection to PHOS. The security boundary is deliberate: the bridge transports the credential, while PHOS resolves AgentIdentity and PermissionProfile and enforces authorization, including camera and Resource permissions, through BearerAgentAuthenticator and AgentApplicationService. The bridge has no identity or permission logic, rejects visible bearer CLI arguments, and does not fall back to an unauthenticated/default identity. Credential rotation or revocation in PHOS invalidates the old bearer; update PHOS_MCP_TOKEN and restart/relaunch the bridge if required to create a new authenticated upstream connection. Hot credential reload is not claimed. Bridge automated validation passed (10 tests); live PHOS/bridge interoperability validation is not yet recorded and remains Stage 3.7 work.

MCP Stage 3.1 establishes an application-level identity boundary. Each inbound MCP request passes through one authentication middleware hook that resolves an immutable provider-neutral AgentIdentity; its permission-profile reference is then used to create the permission-checked AgentApplicationService facade. The transitional LocalAgentAuthenticator resolves every trusted-local client as local-agent with the existing standard profile and verifies no credentials. It preserves prior behavior but is explicitly not production-grade authentication. Credential-backed configuration, per-client authentication, and lifecycle operations are now implemented; expiry policy and external identity providers remain future work.

Sensor availability/freshness transitions are complete: numeric samples remain read-only, while status transitions publish semantic Resource cues. Raspberry Pi validation confirmed direct-HTTP phos://status sleep/wake notifications, phos://physical-context semantic updates, phos://environment availability updates, environment loss/recovery, and motion/IMU availability transitions. The separately owned phos-mcp-bridge was externally validated with a stdio subscription receiving two consecutive phos://status ResourceUpdated notifications. No physical air-quality validation is claimed. A fake-clock test of the monitor sleep loop with a real sensor-service age calculation remains a non-blocking test improvement; _check_sensor_freshness() is automated-tested.

docs.title: PHOS 1.9.0 — Physical Context & Object Awareness
docs.text:
PHOS 1.9.0 adds bounded six-hour, RAM-only physical measurement and semantic transition history, queried through phos_query_measurements and phos_list_physical_transitions. The documented Physical Context Intelligence v0.1 pattern lets external Agents combine those bounded observations with phos_get_physical_context; PHOS supplies facts and summaries, while Agents remain responsible for interpretation and decisions.

It also adds optional, on-demand NanoDet object awareness through phos_get_visible_objects. It reuses the existing VisionPipeline frame owner, is disabled by default, and returns only labels, confidences, and frame freshness—not images, boxes, identities, tracking, or retained object history. The release also corrects the BGR/RGB preview boundary while preserving BGR for OpenCV vision consumers.

docs.title: PHOS 1.8.0 — MCP & Runtime Administration Stabilization
docs.text: PHOS 1.8.0 includes Streamable HTTP MCP semantic tools and Resources, the on-demand permission-controlled phos://vision/snapshot JPEG Resource, and the Web Admin Runtime settings split with immediate Camera Preview/log-level application. Automated coverage verifies the application and permission boundaries; Raspberry Pi camera-snapshot testing confirmed operation with Camera Preview disabled. MCP Stages 2 and 3.3–3.6 are complete; live external multi-agent interoperability validation remains Stage 3.7 work.

docs.title: PHOS 1.7.0 — External Hardware Controller & Semantic LED Control
docs.text: The repository implements the generic phos-hw v1 serial controller boundary, capability discovery, reconnect lifecycle, and controller-backed environmental, air-quality, and IMU semantic providers. It also includes Hardware Controller Web Admin read/configuration paths, capability-aware semantic LED command transport, and POST /api/v1/signal arbitration. These are Raspberry-side implementation records. See the 1.7.0 release record and architecture reference.

docs.title: PHOS 1.4.0 — Voice & Interaction Foundation
docs.text:
PHOS 1.4.0 implements startup/readiness (splash, ready sound and hidden cursor), touch/gesture input, USB microphone capture, canonical 16 kHz PCM16 processing, VAD and bounded pre-roll. Default local Vosk and optional Cartesia Ink batch STT implement the provider-neutral transcription boundary. Local Piper, Cartesia and ElevenLabs TTS adapters feed AudioOutputProvider and the SPEAKING state through /api/v1/speak. YAML is the canonical editable configuration; YAML is the only supported runtime configuration file format.

Transcript-to-intent/command interpretation, wake words, continuous listening, conversational LLM, Home Assistant and MCP events/subscriptions remain deferred.

docs.title: PHOS 1.3.0 release candidate
docs.text:
This is a historical 1.3.0 release-candidate record. The current source version was 1.4.0. Version 1.3.0 added stable Presence and Attention state, transient presence LED reactions, observed facial-expression telemetry, and a bounded expression-reaction policy to the existing Remote API and Web Admin. Automated regression has passed. See release-1.3.0.md for current gates; older release sections below are retained as implementation history, not current release status.

The recommended Raspberry Pi OS installation path is now ./scripts/install-phos.sh. It validates the supported platform, installs the canonical .[all] runtime dependency aggregate, prepares the configured local ONNX model, and performs software-only smoke checks. Follow the hardware setup instructions in the installation guide.

PHOS 1.4.0 Slice 1 adds a local startup splash owned by the existing eye display. Runtime readiness records required display/core and optional Vision, sensors, and LED outcomes as ready, degraded, or failed; normal eyes appear only for ready/degraded startup. Optional local ready sound and face-display-only cursor hiding are configured through the canonical startup section. Physical Pi asset diagnostics now report the resolved splash/sound paths, readability, splash loader result, and aplay outcome. Default PHOS assets are packaged under robot.assets; explicit config overrides remain configuration-relative.

docs.title: Startup-experience Pi integration tests
docs.text: On power-on, confirm the splash appears before normal eyes; it must remain while components initialize. Confirm one ready sound when configured, normal eyes only after ready/degraded state, and a persistent startup error for a critical failure. Verify an unavailable optional sensor permits degraded startup. Move a mouse over the face display to confirm its cursor is hidden, then open Web Admin and confirm the browser cursor remains normal. Touch/gesture behavior is documented separately from this startup test sequence.

docs.title: Core and behavior
docs.text:
• Event bus and explicit RobotState state machine.
  • BehaviorEngine under src/robot/core/behavior_engine.py.
  • Skin-owned Physical Personality v0.2 is an IDLE-only policy: analytical, playful, and calm select bounded blink/gaze timing internally (the missing-field fallback is analytical). Analytical uses 4.8–7.2 s blinks, 4.0–7.0 s gaze rests, 1.4–2.3 s holds and a 1.5% double-blink chance; playful uses 2.4–4.2 s, 1.5–3.2 s, 0.65–1.25 s and 18%; calm uses 5.5–8.0 s, 4.8–8.0 s, 1.8–3.0 s and 4%. A double blink has a bounded 90–220 ms open pause (preset-specific). Gaze targets hold, return to neutral, then rest. Attention, vision tracking, IMU motion, explicit reactions, non-IDLE states, and skin changes cancel pending personality sequences. In global appearance mode, the persisted appearance.global_skin_id selects the complete Skin identity (appearance, palette, and personality); no selected Skin retains legacy global appearance with the analytical fallback. Focused automated coverage is present. User-confirmed Raspberry Pi observations cover visible preset differences, persistence, manual application, and IMU integration; broader Vision/attention integration and performance testing remain planned work.
  • Environmental behavior is implemented through EnvironmentalInterpreter: confirmed, hysteretic temperature and CCS811 eCO2/TVOC context becomes EnvironmentalState, then a BehaviorEngine eye/LED accent. Missing, stale or unavailable data produces no alarm.
  • Environmental overlays are additive display decoration: the interpreter also exposes independently confirmed temperature (warm/cold) and air-quality (warning/bad) intents, allowing sweat/snow and haze to coexist while the existing single priority EnvironmentalState continues to drive eyes and LEDs.
  • Behavior produces FaceState and handles blink/idle gaze.
  • Robot states include IDLE, LISTENING, THINKING, SPEAKING, SLEEPING and ERROR.
  • Presence/Attention vertical slice is implemented and covered by hardware-free lifecycle tests: provider-neutral selected-face observations use confirmed Presence edges and Attention IDLE → ACQUIRING → TRACKING → LOST → IDLE. It supplies semantic gaze and optional configured LED enter/leave transients through BehaviorEngine and FaceState, without identity recognition.

docs.title: UI / eyes
docs.text:
• UI-neutral FaceState and expression/blink enums.
  • The manually selectable expression set is neutral, happy, curious, surprised, sad, angry, focused, tired, confused, scared and skeptical. sleepy and worried remain renderer vocabulary for existing state/reaction behavior, rather than manual commands. Robot state and expression remain independent: for example, focused can be selected while PHOS is thinking without changing that state. Manual selection persists until explicitly replaced. The shared canonical expression profile and geometry path drives both live Tk eyes and Appearance Preview; automatic BehaviorEngine selection of the manually selectable expressions is deferred.
  • Every expression supports the configured/custom iris color. HAPPY's blue eye-body accent and SURPRISED's yellow eye-body accent remain specific semantic exceptions; expression geometry is the primary visual language, not a general emotion-to-color mapping. FURIOUS and expression intensity are not implemented.
  • Eye renderer/display runtime with smooth frame updates.
  • Standalone eye demo under src/robot/ui/demo.py.
