robot.__version__ in src/robot/__init__.py is authoritative. Setuptools derives metadata from that literal; do not add another independently maintained version. Source checkouts use config/phos.yaml; wheels install the same YAML asset under the environment's share/phos/config/ data directory. Explicit --config remains the supported deployment boundary; no alternate schema is introduced. The pinned Python 3.11+ web snapshot is requirements-web.txt; platform camera dependencies remain managed by Raspberry Pi OS. See the release record.

robot.lifecycle is the reusable lifecycle policy boundary. Its fixed operations are status/reload/restart; it never accepts arbitrary commands or configuration paths from callers. The web worker uses robot.lifecycle_channel to reach the parent-owned service. Confirmation/authentication remain adapter responsibilities; validation and restart capability policy are shared. Test both the service and adapter guards. Infrastructure service markers are deployment metadata, not ordinary JSON settings. No new runtime configuration section is needed.

docs.title: Environmental configuration migration
docs.text:
For an existing BME280 deployment, rename sensors.bme280 to sensors.environmental, retain its four existing values and add "type": "bme280". Do not retain both blocks. To use BMP280 choose "type": "bmp280"; humidity is unsupported. The Python RuntimeConfig fields now use the environmental_ prefix.

When updating a deployment without sensor settings, merge the complete sensors object from config/phos.yaml into its existing configuration, preserving other settings. The new section and all five fields are required even when disabled. As with previous schema additions, missing fields fail validation; no silent overlay/migration or second set of defaults is introduced. run_pi.sh preserves deployed JSON and does not perform this merge. Validate locally before restarting the service. No new CLI flags are added. Save/Reload classify every sensor difference as restart-required; unrelated services are not restarted by either action.

Hardware-free sensor checks: .venv/bin/python -m pytest -q tests/test_sensors.py. The adapter uses lazy optional imports; disabled operation and ordinary tests need neither Linux I2C access nor the driver packages. Fake drivers test address, chip ID, calibration and unit mapping; the service tests failure recovery, staleness, polling and bounded shutdown independently of physical hardware.

docs.title: ENS160/AHT21 controller telemetry
docs.text: ENS160 and AHT21 are acquired by the ESP32 and delivered through the controller protocol. sensors.ens160 configures controller-backed air-quality enablement; the public runtime records are sensors.ens160 and sensors.aht21. Tests should exercise protocol decoding, validity, per-measurement freshness and controller generation retirement rather than direct Pi I2C drivers.

docs.title: MPU-6050 configuration migration
docs.text: Merge the complete sensors.imu block from canonical JSON into an existing deployment, preserving the environmental configuration. The typed surface uses the imu_ prefix. All four fields are required even when disabled and are restart-only. IMUReading contains finite acceleration values in m/s² and angular velocity values in °/s. It has no persisted calibration state: the adapter applies fixed factory scale factors only. Run .venv/bin/python -m pytest -q tests/test_imu.py before Pi validation.

docs.title: Tilt interpretation configuration migration
docs.text: Add tilt_exit_threshold_m_s2, lateral_axis and forward_axis from canonical sensors.imu.motion to existing deployments; missing fields fail validation. The existing tilt enter key is preserved but now refers to a normalized gravity component. Review enter/exit together. For responsive operation, adopt the canonical IMU poll interval and confirmation duration; polling requires restart, motion thresholds/mounting require only reload. See the installation guide for axis verification and DEBUG diagnostics.

docs.title: External hardware controller administration
docs.text: Web Admin's Hardware Controller page edits the canonical hardware_controller configuration through the application/lifecycle boundary. Changing the enabled state, serial device, or baud rate closes the prior session and starts a fresh reconnect/handshake session without restarting PHOS; timing changes are applied to the existing service. It discovers serial ports only through the parent application service; the browser never inspects device files. The canonical settings are enabled, transport (currently serial only), serial.device, serial.baud_rate, reconnect.delay_seconds, and heartbeat interval_seconds/timeout_seconds; timeout must exceed interval. These are connection settings, not controller-firmware or LED-animation settings. The page also exposes controller-owned read-only connection state and a bounded, in-memory RX/TX diagnostic buffer. Diagnostics are not persisted, heartbeat rows are hidden by default, and raw frames are bounded to the phos-hw frame limit.

docs.title: GitHub Actions software validation
docs.text:
PHOS CI runs on pull requests targeting dev or main, every push to dev, and after a GitHub Release is published. It runs the complete software-compatible pytest suite, Python compilation, and a strict MkDocs build. Reports are available from the workflow run as a JUnit XML file and a 30-day artifact, including command output and execution environment details.

Release validation checks out the published tag, resolves its commit, and fails unless that commit is reachable from main. It runs after publication, so it reports invalid release provenance but cannot prevent the initial publication. PASS means the automated software checks completed; FAIL means one failed; SKIPPED is reported by pytest; INCOMPLETE means a report was not produced. Every summary explicitly states that Raspberry Pi hardware validation was not run. Test GPIO, camera, display, audio, I2C wiring, and physical performance manually on the Pi.

Repository administrators must enable required pull requests, require the software-tests check, require branches to be current, and restrict direct pushes on dev and main. The separate MCP bridge repository is not checked out by PHOS CI; add bridge CI only once a pinned, CI-accessible source revision is available.

docs.title: Discover PHOS
docs.text:
Bringing AI agents into the physical world.

Eyes, voice and senses for AI agents. PHOS is an open-source, bidirectional physical I/O layer for AI agents, powered by the Model Context Protocol.

docs.title: Give your agent a physical interface
docs.text:
An agent can read selected physical context and communicate through a local expressive face, configured speech, and supported LED signals. People can notice activity or a request for attention beyond a chat window. PHOS handles devices, context, permissions, and execution; your agent supplies reasoning and decisions.

Bring your own agent. Bring your own hardware. Connect through a compatible MCP client. Use supported Raspberry Pi peripherals or an external controller implementing the phos-hw v1 protocol. The runtime targets Raspberry Pi 3; controller extensibility does not imply support for every board or sensor.

docs.title: Perceive physical context
docs.text: Read available temperature, humidity, pressure, air-quality indicators, motion, anonymous presence, attention, and observed expressions. Measurements are accompanied by availability and semantic context where implemented. Authorized camera snapshots and optional on-demand object labels are separate interfaces. See core capabilities.

docs.title: React to meaningful changes
docs.text: Subscription-capable clients receive resource change cues and read updated context. PHOS reports selected semantic transitions rather than pushing every sensor sample. The external host or agent decides whether to reason or act; notifications are best-effort and have no replay. See MCP integration.

docs.title: Express through a physical presence
docs.text: Animated eyes combine blink, local gaze behavior, expressions, and state visuals. Agents can request supported expressions and temporary thinking visuals, speak through configured TTS, or signal through available controller LEDs. There is no direct MCP gaze or raw LED control. See how PHOS works.

docs.title: Share controlled access
docs.text: Register distinct agent identities and credentials with observer or standard profiles. PHOS checks resource reads and tool operations through application services. Agents share the physical outputs; external applications coordinate their own tasks. See agent access.

docs.title: Standalone operation
docs.text:
PHOS can also operate locally without an external agent. Its runtime renders eyes, responds to supported touch gestures, manages robot state, and applies configured sensor reactions. Optional voice services provide bounded microphone sessions, STT, TTS/playback, and the deterministic English/Italian voice command catalog. End-to-end conversational LLM operation, wake words, and continuous listening remain outside the delivered local voice path.

Use this mode for a local expressive display, hardware checks, or personalization. Both standalone and agent-connected operation require the local runtime. Installation explains setup; Web Admin provides configuration and operational controls, and skins personalize the face.

docs.title: See PHOS and choose a path
docs.text:
Watch the official demonstrations on the homepage or visit the PHOS YouTube channel.

  • Explore use cases
  • Build PHOS
  • Understand hardware integration
  • Build integrations and contribute

The public overview pages explain PHOS at a glance. The documents below are the canonical engineering references: they contain the detailed commands, thresholds, configuration fields and operating limits that the overview intentionally does not duplicate.

These documents are written for users and contributors who need technical detail. Release notes distinguish implemented source paths from physical verification.

docs.title: Environmental awareness
docs.text:
CONTEXT, NOT RAW CONTROL

Environmental readings are confirmed and interpreted before they influence the face, ring or overlays.

BME280 / BMP280 · controller ENS160/AHT21 → EnvironmentalInterpreter → Semantic state & overlay intents → BehaviorEngine / FaceState → Eyes · LEDs · overlays

PHOS interprets environmental context rather than mapping raw values straight to a renderer. Optional BME280/BMP280 readings provide temperature (plus pressure, and humidity only on BME280). Controller-backed ENS160 provides TVOC, AQI-UBA and estimated / equivalent CO2 (eCO2), not direct NDIR CO2; AHT21 provides separately fresh controller temperature and humidity.

EnvironmentalInterpreter confirms and recovers semantic states with hysteresis: NORMAL, COLD, WARM, AIR_QUALITY_WARNING and AIR_QUALITY_BAD. Missing, stale or unavailable readings do not create an alarm. Partial sensor availability remains useful, while ENS160 warm-up withholds only air-quality rules—not fresh temperature context.

The single priority state drives persistent eye/LED behavior. Independently confirmed overlay intents are additive: warm conditions can add sweat, cold can add snow/ice, and air quality can add haze. Temperature and air-quality overlays can coexist in a shared safe display band.

Thresholds and physical setup remain in the canonical architecture, hardware and installation guides.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
CAPABILITY MAP

Perceive physical context, react through compatible external clients, and express agent activity through a local interface. Capabilities depend on the hardware and providers enabled in your build. Start with connecting an agent, then use the subsystem guides below for setup and limits.

docs.title: Agent-facing capabilities
docs.text: Capability Practical value Details Physical awareness Read measurements and semantic context without managing device drivers. MCP resources and tools Event-driven interaction Receive selected semantic-change cues, then read current context. Subscriptions and lifecycle Physical expression Request supported expressions, temporary thinking visuals, speech, and available LED signals. MCP tool catalog Hardware extensibility Connect supported Pi peripherals or protocol-compatible controllers. Hardware architecture Agent independence and multiple identities Give separate agents credentials and permission profiles on a shared runtime. Controlled access

docs.title: Expressive animated eyes
docs.text: An independent renderer provides smooth eye animation, blink and idle gaze, semantic visual accents, selectable iris themes and optional local camera picture-in-picture.

docs.title: Face tracking and expression observations
docs.text: The Pi Camera pipeline selects and tracks a face, maps its position to bounded pupil gaze, and can use local ONNX or optional AWS expression providers. Stable observations—not raw labels—reach behavior.

docs.title: Presence and attention
docs.text: Confirmed face presence produces edge-triggered enter/leave semantics. A provider-neutral attention state acquires, tracks, holds loss and returns to idle, driving semantic gaze and optional configured LED sweeps. It is not face recognition, biometric identity, eye-contact, multi-person arbitration, or voice engagement.

docs.title: Motion awareness
docs.text: Optional MPU-6050/GY-521 support turns six-axis readings into confirmed STILL, MOVING, directional tilt, SHAKE and IMPACT observations with temporary, directional eye and LED intent.

docs.title: Environmental awareness
docs.text: Optional BME280/BMP280 and controller-backed ENS160/AHT21 services feed EnvironmentalInterpreter. Confirmed temperature and air-quality context can drive semantic eye/LED behavior and additive sweat, snow/ice and haze overlays.

docs.title: Visual source arbitration
docs.text: Manual, environmental or PHOS-state persistent visual sources establish a baseline. IMU and higher-priority robot events are transient overrides; the resolved persistent source returns afterward.

docs.title: Voice & Speech
docs.text: An explicit microphone session uses energy VAD and a provider-neutral STT boundary: Local/Vosk is the default and Cartesia Ink is optional batch STT. Local/Piper, Cartesia, and ElevenLabs TTS integration use AudioOutputProvider; supported Voice & Speech provider/output changes activate live and persist.

docs.title: Face-display touch telemetry
docs.text: Completed taps, double-taps, long presses and horizontal swipes are recognized locally as semantic input. The last valid gesture is observable through the shared runtime snapshot, Remote API and read-only Web Admin diagnostics; raw pointer events are never exposed.

docs.title: WS2812B visual feedback
docs.text: An optional WS2812B ring connects to the ESP32 controller. PHOS sends resolved phos-hw v1 semantic LED commands over an active serial connection; firmware drives the ring after advertising LED capability.

docs.title: Web Admin and canonical configuration
docs.text: An authenticated trusted-LAN editor saves the active validated configuration source, normally config/phos.yaml. Voice & Speech shows configured and active provider state and applies supported STT/TTS/audio changes live; other subsystem settings retain their documented reload or restart policy.

docs.title: Remote API & OpenAPI
docs.text:
Explore the Remote API

PHOS exposes a versioned local REST API for robot status, health, environmental and motion state, capabilities, semantic expressions, visual source control and face overlays. The API includes OpenAPI 3.x documentation, Swagger UI and structured JSON errors, and reuses the same application-service boundary as the Web Admin.

docs.title: Explicitly planned, not delivered
docs.text: Conversational LLM operation, wake-word and continuous listening, and Home Assistant are deferred. The supported deterministic English/Italian voice commands are available. MCP tools, resources, and resource-change subscriptions are implemented; see MCP & AI Agent Integration for their bounded semantics. Existing interfaces or scaffolding are not evidence of an end-to-end delivered feature. Read the roadmap.

docs.title: Hardware Bill of Materials (BOM)
docs.text: Start with a Raspberry Pi and display for a desktop PHOS build, then add a camera, voice hardware, sensors, and an external controller as needed. The tables separate the core setup from optional capabilities and list the interfaces used by the current providers.

docs.title: Choose a build tier
docs.text:
Tier Parts Enables 1 — Core / minimal build Raspberry Pi, microSD, power supply, display and cables; camera for vision Animated eyes and UI, plus camera observations when configured 2 — Voice & audio add-on Tier 1 plus microphone and audio output Bounded STT/voice-command sessions and TTS playback 3 — Sensors & external controller Tier 1 plus your choice of I2C sensors, ESP32 and LEDs; add Tier 2 for speech Environmental and motion context, air-quality telemetry, and semantic LED feedback

  • Start with the face

    Install Raspberry Pi OS with a graphical desktop and connect the display. The camera is required for vision, but can be omitted for an eyes-only build.

  • Add speech

    Connect a microphone and speaker, then select the STT and TTS providers in Voice & Speech.

  • Expand physical context

    Add local I2C modules or an ESP32 running the official phos-esp32 firmware. Enable one configured capability at a time.

docs.title: Tier 1 — Core / minimal build
docs.text:
Component Quantity Interface / selection notes Raspberry Pi 1 Raspberry Pi 3 is the repository baseline; a 3 Model B+ is a build choice in that family. A Pi 4 or another Debian-based board is an alternative build target that needs its own OS, camera and display setup; installer architecture checks accept armv7l and aarch64, not arbitrary boards. microSD card 1 Suggested starting size: 16 GB or larger, Class 10. This is a planning recommendation, not a runtime-enforced minimum; allow space for OS packages and local speech/vision models. Power supply 1 Use a regulated supply and cable appropriate to the selected Pi and the attached USB load. Account separately for display and LED power. Display 1 Reference size/resolution: 5-inch, 800×600. Choose HDMI or DSI according to the Pi and panel, with matching display power and cables. PHOS renders through the local graphical desktop; it has no panel-specific driver. Raspberry Pi Camera Module and ribbon cable 1 for vision CSI camera supported by the installed Picamera2/libcamera stack. Select the ribbon/connector for your board; the reference camera model is unspecified. Network connection 1 during setup Ethernet or Wi-Fi for cloning, package installation, and optional LAN administration or agent access.

Follow Build PHOS and the installation guide. Touch gestures additionally require touchscreen input recognized by the OS.

docs.title: Tier 2 — Voice & audio add-on
docs.text:
Component Quantity Interface / purpose USB microphone or compatible audio input 1 Input device recognized by the configured capture stack; capture is resampled to canonical 16 kHz PCM16 mono for STT. Speaker with an audio output path 1 HDMI/display audio, supported USB audio, or the selected Pi's 3.5 mm output. A passive speaker needs an appropriate amplifier. Configure ALSA aplay or PipeWire pw-play output.

STT supports local Vosk and optional Cartesia. TTS supports local Piper, Cartesia, and ElevenLabs, with synthesis and playback configured separately. Install local model assets or configure the selected cloud provider's credentials through the external secrets boundary. See Voice and TTS.

docs.title: Tier 3 — Sensors & external microcontroller add-ons
docs.text:
Select only the modules needed for your build. Pi I2C providers use bus 1; ENS160/AHT21 use the controller's I2C bus.

Component Quantity Interface / addresses Measurements or function ESP32 board and USB data cable 1 for controller-backed hardware USB/serial, phos-hw v1 UTF-8 JSONL; default host settings /dev/ttyACM0, 115200 baud Sensor telemetry, capability discovery, heartbeat/reconnect, and semantic LED commands. Flash the official phos-esp32 firmware. Bosch BME280 or BMP280 breakout 1 optional Pi I2C bus 1, 0x76 or 0x77; 3.3 V-compatible logic Both: temperature and pressure. BME280 also measures humidity; BMP280 has no humidity output. Select the matching type in configuration. ENS160 + AHT21 combo module 1 optional ESP32 I2C: ENS160 0x53 or 0x52, AHT21 0x38 ENS160: estimated eCO2, TVOC, AQI-UBA 1–5, validity and compensation status. AHT21: temperature and humidity. No direct Pi I2C provider. MPU6050 / GY-521 breakout 1 optional Pi I2C bus 1, 0x68 or 0x69 Six-axis acceleration and angular velocity, interpreted motion and tilt. Configure mounting axes. WS2812B addressable RGB LED ring 1 optional ESP32 firmware-selected output; phos-hw v1 semantic LED commands over Pi-to-ESP32 USB/serial Firmware drives the ring. Set LED count, pin, channel ordering, and power to match the fitted hardware; an active controller connection and advertised LED capability are required. Jumper wires, connectors and mounting hardware As needed Match the breakout pinout and enclosure Secure connections and consistent sensor orientation.

ENS160 eCO2 is an estimated CO2 equivalent, not a direct NDIR CO2 measurement. See hardware wiring, motion setup, and the controller protocol.

docs.title: Wiring map
docs.text:
Flash the ESP32 using the build/upload instructions in phosairobot/phos-esp32. Select the sensor wiring and LED pin/count for your board to enable ENS160 + AHT21 telemetry and WS2812B semantic LED control, then follow the PHOS controller setup.

  storage[MicroSD and Pi power] --> pi[Raspberry Pi]
  camera[Raspberry Pi Camera] -->|CSI / Picamera2| pi
  pi -->|HDMI or OS-supported DSI| display[800x600 display]
  mic[Microphone] -->|USB / audio capture| pi
  pi -->|HDMI / USB / 3.5 mm audio| speaker[Speaker / audio output]
  sensors[BME280 or BMP280 / MPU6050] <-->|Pi I2C bus 1| pi
  pi <-->|USB serial / phos-hw v1 JSONL| esp[ESP32 controller]

docs.title: Wiring & configuration checklist
docs.text:
1. Power off before wiring. Check each breakout's supply requirements, labels, logic levels, and schematic; Pi GPIO/I2C uses 3.3 V logic.
  2. Enable Pi I2C for local sensors and confirm their configured addresses. Keep ENS160/AHT21 on the ESP32 bus and provide a common ground for connected hardware.
  3. Check display, camera and audio devices through the OS, then run PHOS from the local graphical desktop.
  4. For ESP32, use a USB data cable, the correct serial device and permissions, matching baud rate, and firmware implementing the documented v1 messages.
  5. Set the ESP32 firmware's actual LED pin/count and power requirements. Use a suitable external LED supply and level shifting where required; do not power a ring from a GPIO pin.
  6. Enable the selected provider, restart or reload as documented, then inspect availability, freshness and readings in Web Admin before adding another module.

Enable only the hardware you have connected

Edit the canonical config/phos.yaml after wiring. Optional sensors, the controller, LED ring, camera processing, voice and TTS start disabled. Configure sensors.environmental, sensors.ens160, sensors.imu, and hardware_controller for the selected path. The ESP32 ring requires hardware_controller.enabled: true and controller-advertised LED capability; keep legacy led_ring.enabled: false. Controller-backed sensors use provider: controller and an enabled controller. Keep credentials outside runtime configuration.

docs.title: External hardware controllers — phos-hw v1
docs.text: PHOS implements the phos-hw v1 external-controller boundary. The official companion ESP32 firmware is available at phosairobot/phos-esp32, providing ENS160 + AHT21 telemetry and WS2812B semantic LED control over USB/serial JSONL.

docs.title: A hardware boundary independent of the agent
docs.text:
A compatible controller lets an agent use physical context without learning its board, sensor bus, pins, or firmware. PHOS accepts supported observations through phos-hw v1, adds availability and semantic interpretation, and exposes the result through MCP. In the other direction, PHOS resolves permitted LED intent before firmware executes it.

phos-hw v1 is the hardware communication protocol; MCP is the agent-facing protocol. They serve different boundaries. The Raspberry Pi runs PHOS and owns semantics. The external controller acquires sensors and drives its supported outputs. It does not replace the Pi runtime.

flowchart TD
  sensors[Physical sensors] --> controller[Compatible microcontroller]
  controller -->|phos-hw v1 observations over serial| adapter[Pi controller adapter]
  adapter --> context[PHOS semantic services and context]
  context -->|MCP resources and notifications| agent[External MCP client / agent]
  agent -->|MCP tools| services[Permission-checked application services]
  services --> intent[Runtime LED arbitration]
  intent -->|phos-hw v1 set_led_animation| controller
  controller --> leds[Physical LED output]

ESP32 is the official reference firmware implementation. The protocol is not ESP32-specific: a developer could implement it on Arduino, RP2040, or STM32 hardware with a suitable serial transport and firmware. These are potential ports, not supported board integrations. A port must implement the actual frame, capability, freshness, and command contracts below; protocol extensibility does not make arbitrary sensors automatically available through MCP.

docs.title: Flash the companion firmware
docs.text:
1. Open phos-esp32 and follow its current build and flashing instructions for your ESP32 board.
  2. Configure the firmware's sensor wiring and WS2812B data pin/count for the attached hardware, then build and upload as described there. Keep ENS160 and AHT21 on the ESP32 I2C bus and the LED ring on the ESP32 output.
  3. Connect the flashed ESP32 to the Pi with a USB data cable. Configure hardware_controller.enabled, hardware_controller.serial.device, and hardware_controller.serial.baud_rate in PHOS to match the connection.
  4. Confirm capability discovery, fresh sensor telemetry, and semantic LED output. Use the installation checks for the PHOS side of the connection.

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text:
The Raspberry Pi owns high-level semantics, state, arbitration, and application services. The controller owns supported physical execution and sensor acquisition. It does not decide robot behavior or expose a second Web/API/MCP control plane.

This separation keeps hardware modular, isolates physical execution, supports reconnection after transport failure, and lets a controller implementation be replaced or extended without moving PHOS semantics into firmware.

docs.title: Connection and lifecycle
docs.text:
Enable hardware_controller with the configured serial transport, device, and baud rate. PHOS performs capability discovery, sends heartbeats, reconnects after transport failure using the configured delay, and exposes bounded connection status/recent diagnostics in Web Admin. Controller transport failure does not give Web clients direct serial access.

hardware_controller.serial.dtr and .rts default to false. PHOS configures these values before opening pySerial so ESP32 USB-UART auto-reset circuitry is not unintentionally driven by the host's default asserted control lines. Boards with a documented different requirement may opt in through the same Hardware Controller configuration; changing either setting reconnects the controller and may briefly interrupt sensor readings and controller-backed LED output. Verify the selected levels on the target controller board.

docs.title: WS2812B ring connection
docs.text:
The WS2812B addressable RGB LED ring connects to and is driven by the ESP32 controller. The Raspberry Pi sends resolved phos-hw v1 semantic set_led_animation commands over USB/serial; firmware owns the data pin, pixel count, channel ordering, and animation timing.

Enable hardware_controller.enabled in config/phos.yaml and configure hardware_controller.serial.device and hardware_controller.serial.baud_rate for the attached ESP32. PHOS emits LED commands only when that serial session is connected and advertises LED support: a nonzero led_count, a nonzero led.count, or "led" in the payload's capabilities list.

Keep the separate legacy led_ring.enabled setting false. Its pin/count settings do not configure ESP32 firmware. On disconnect, controller output becomes unavailable; after a new LED capability report, PHOS reapplies the resolved intent. See the installation steps and electrical guidance.

docs.title: Message envelope
docs.text:
Messages are framed JSON objects with protocol: "phos-hw", version: 1, a type, optional correlation fields, and an object payload. Capability reports describe controller-supported features. Controller sensor_update and motion_update messages feed the same semantic snapshots used by local sensor providers; semantic LED commands are resolved by PHOS before the controller executes timing/physical mapping.

See Architecture: external controller protocol for exact message contracts, validation, bounds, failure handling, and LED arbitration. See Development for configuration and Web Admin behavior.

docs.title: Verified v1 commands and messages
docs.text:
phos-hw v1 uses UTF-8 JSON Lines: one bounded JSON object per newline. Every message has protocol: "phos-hw", version: 1, type, and object payload; id, reply_to, and timestamp_ms are optional correlation fields. PHOS starts a reader before capability discovery, retries discovery until a capabilities report arrives, sends ping as its heartbeat, and reconnects after a transport failure using the configured delay. A controller heartbeat updates the recorded heartbeat status. On disconnect, PHOS retains bounded diagnostics but disables active controller LED output.

Malformed lines remain rejected. Their bounded diagnostics identify whether UTF-8 or JSON parsing failed, the frame length, a short hexadecimal prefix, and the connection generation; complete untrusted frames are not retained. Valid later lines received in the same serial read continue through normal protocol validation. ESP32 boot/debug output must not share the protocol UART, and every firmware protocol write must emit one complete UTF-8 JSON object followed by a newline.

For every enabled controller-provided environmental sensor, firmware must also send a valid sensor_update periodically when its value is unchanged. PHOS uses each accepted sensor-family update as freshness evidence and marks the family stale after its configured stale_after_seconds; a heartbeat or IMU frame cannot refresh environmental data. Use a refresh interval comfortably below that timeout (at most half the timeout is recommended; 15 seconds or less for the standard 30-second setting). This preserves truthful detection of a stopped sensor while allowing a stable temperature or pressure value to stay available.

docs.title: Targeted malformed-frame diagnostics
docs.text:
PHOS normally keeps controller debug logging disabled. To enable bounded serial diagnostics only (without changing global logging.level), create a temporary user-service override on the Pi:

mkdir -p ~/.config/systemd/user/phos.service.d
printf '[Service]\nEnvironment=PHOS_CONTROLLER_DEBUG=1\n' > ~/.config/systemd/user/phos.service.d/controller-debug.conf
systemctl --user daemon-reload
systemctl --user restart phos.service
journalctl --user -u phos.service -f --no-pager

Look for PHOS CONTROLLER: rejected frame diagnostics entries. They contain only parse category, frame length, a 24-byte hexadecimal prefix, and connection generation. To restore ordinary logging:

rm ~/.config/systemd/user/phos.service.d/controller-debug.conf
systemctl --user daemon-reload
systemctl --user restart phos.service

High-rate orientation telemetry remains off when PHOS_CONTROLLER_DEBUG=1. For a separate, temporary IMU investigation only, add Environment=PHOS_CONTROLLER_IMU_DEBUG=1 to the same override, reload systemd and restart; remove that line again afterward.

The protocol recognizes the following vocabulary. “Recognized” is not the same as “currently emitted by PHOS”: the current serial adapter transmits only request_capabilities, ping, and resolved set_led_animation.

Protocol name Direction Purpose / data Response or unavailable behavior request_capabilities Pi → controller Starts (and resynchronizes) discovery; empty payload may carry an id. Controller supplies capabilities for every request and resumes/reaffirms telemetry for the current host session. PHOS retries until a capabilities report arrives, even if stale telemetry or heartbeats are already arriving. capabilities controller → Pi Controller-defined feature metadata, including optional sensor/LED support. Activates session capabilities; LEDs require advertised support. ping Pi → controller PHOS heartbeat; empty payload. Peer activity keeps the session healthy; v1 requires no separate pong. heartbeat controller → Pi Controller liveness cue. Updates PHOS's recorded heartbeat time. sensor_update controller → Pi Semantic sensor/value/unit or supported push event. Valid updates enter existing semantic services; invalid updates are rejected safely. sensor_status controller → Pi Additive ENS160 status: sensor: "ens160", validity integer 0–3, and compensation_active boolean. Sent on change and at the bounded air-quality refresh cadence. Codes are normal, warm-up, startup, and invalid respectively; old controllers may omit it. motion_update controller → Pi Semantic motion state and intensity. Exact validated values update the IMU service. orientation_update controller → Pi Finite x, y, z acceleration and angular-velocity vectors. Exact validated vectors update IMU telemetry. set_led_animation Pi → controller PHOS-resolved LED animation semantics. Sent only for an active LED-capable session; otherwise unavailable. hello, controller_status, warning, error, ack controller → Pi Recognized lifecycle/diagnostic/acknowledgement vocabulary. Recorded as bounded diagnostics; no PHOS semantic mapping currently. configure_sensor_reporting, stop_led_animation, set_led_brightness, clear_led Pi → controller Reserved recognized command vocabulary. Not transmitted by the current PHOS adapter.

Unknown message types, unsupported versions, malformed JSON, and invalid validated payloads receive bounded protocol errors. Unknown top-level fields are ignored; arbitrary controller data never reaches PHOS services.

docs.title: Verified JSON Lines examples
docs.text:
Each complete object below is followed by a newline on the wire.

{"protocol":"phos-hw","version":1,"type":"request_capabilities","id":"phos-1-cap-1","payload":{}}

{"protocol":"phos-hw","version":1,"type":"sensor_update","payload":{"sensor":"temperature","value":24.8,"unit":"c"}}

{"protocol":"phos-hw","version":1,"type":"set_led_animation","payload":{"animation":"breathe","color":"#42a5ff","brightness":0.5,"period_ms":1200}}

docs.title: Sensor and motion observations
docs.text:
Controller-backed observations enter the same semantic services as local providers. BME280/BMP280 can provide temperature and pressure; only BME280 supplies humidity. ENS160 reports eCO2 (an estimated CO2 equivalent, not direct CO2), TVOC in ppb and AQI-UBA on its 1–5 scale; AHT21 supplies controller-provenance temperature and humidity used for ENS160 compensation. MPU6050 telemetry is represented by semantic motion updates and/or acceleration and angular-velocity vectors. Physical hardware, wiring, and firmware support vary by installation.

The accepted semantic sensor values are temperature in c, pressure in hpa, humidity in %, eCO2 in ppm, TVOC in ppb, and the push event {"sensor":"push","event":"pressed"}. Motion states are stationary, moving, directional tilt, shake, or impact, with low, medium, or high intensity. PHOS owns the meaning of those observations after they cross the protocol boundary.

docs.title: Operational status
docs.text: The PHOS controller protocol, reconnect lifecycle, capability discovery, and controller-backed sensor/LED integration are implemented and automatically tested. Use the official companion firmware and follow the wiring and protocol setup instructions.

docs.title: Bring your own hardware through defined interfaces
docs.text:
PHOS separates its Raspberry Pi runtime from physical-device adapters and external controller firmware. Agents read shared physical context through MCP; they do not need a BME280 driver, an ESP32 SDK, or serial access. Supported measurements, interpreted conditions, and availability retain the same application-service boundary regardless of the configured provider.

The Pi 3 and 800×600 display are the reference runtime platform. An external microcontroller is optional. The implemented phos-hw v1 protocol uses serial UTF-8 JSON Lines with capability discovery, heartbeat, reconnect handling, sensor observations, and resolved semantic LED commands. ESP32 is its reference controller implementation, not a dependency of every PHOS build.

See the controller architecture and protocol for sensor mapping and porting requirements. Support for a protocol does not imply support for every microcontroller or sensor. The table below identifies the existing hardware paths; wiring details remain the setup reference.

PHYSICAL PLATFORM

PHOS targets a Raspberry Pi 3 and keeps hardware-specific access behind providers/adapters. Optional devices are disabled by default; enable them after wiring and configuration.

Start with the Hardware BOM to choose a core build, audio add-ons, and optional sensors or an ESP32 controller.

For the controller build, flash the official phos-esp32 firmware following its build/upload instructions. It provides ENS160 + AHT21 telemetry and WS2812B semantic LED control; complete the Pi-side setup.

Component What PHOS uses it for Raspberry Pi 3 Main computer, runtime and hardware controller. 5-inch 800×600 display / touchscreen Animated face and eye output, plus local touch gestures where available. Raspberry Pi Camera Face detection, tracking and optional expression observations. USB microphone Voice capture, VAD, and provider-neutral speech-to-text input. HDMI/display audio path Reference playback path for PHOS text-to-speech output. BME280 / BMP280 Temperature and pressure; BME280 also supplies humidity for environmental context. ENS160 + AHT21 Controller-backed eCO2/TVOC/AQI-UBA plus temperature/humidity; eCO2 is not direct CO2. GY-521 / MPU-6050 Acceleration and angular velocity for interpreted motion/tilt events. WS2812B RGB LED ring Connected to the ESP32; driven via phos-hw v1 semantic LED commands.

Find wiring, voltage limits, and I²C addresses in the hardware guide.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text:
PHOS runs on Raspberry Pi; external controllers are an optional integration boundary. The hardware-agnostic phos-hw v1 serial protocol carries accepted sensor observations and semantic LED commands between a compatible controller and the local runtime. MCP separately connects external agents to PHOS's permission-checked services. ESP32 is the reference controller implementation. See hardware architecture and the controller protocol before extending a build.

Use the Hardware BOM to plan parts and build tiers; this page provides the wiring, addresses, power, and device setup details.

The official companion firmware is phosairobot/phos-esp32. Follow its board-specific build and flashing instructions for ENS160 + AHT21 telemetry and WS2812B semantic LED control, then enable the serial connection through the controller setup guide.

Current environmental baseline: ENS160 and AHT21 share the ESP32 I2C bus (ENS160 0x53 or 0x52; AHT21 0x38). The ESP32 publishes phos-hw v1 sensor_update and ENS160 sensor_status JSONL telemetry. The Pi owns freshness, validity, reconnect/session isolation and semantic decisions; it does not poll these devices directly.

This document records the physical hardware that is part of PHOS or has been selected for a future integration milestone.

The table identifies current adapters and planned components. Choose parts with implemented providers for the capabilities you want to enable.

docs.title: Installed / available
docs.text: Component Current state Interface / power Intended role Notes Raspberry Pi Available Raspberry Pi 3 Main PHOS computer and hardware controller Primary target platform Display Available / working 5 inch, 800x600 PHOS face / eyes Exact electrical/display interface should remain documented from the real build Microphone Available Exact model/interface TBD Future voice input Exact model/interface still to document Speaker Planned TBD Future voice output Not yet specified Raspberry Pi Camera Available / working Raspberry Pi camera interface Vision and face tracking Already used by the current PHOS Vision stack BME280 / BMP280 Integrated optional sensor I2C bus 1, 3.3 V logic Temperature, relative humidity where supported, atmospheric pressure Verify actual breakout/address for each installation ENS160 + AHT21 ESP32 controller telemetry I2C on controller eCO2/TVOC/AQI-UBA plus temperature/humidity ENS160 eCO2 is not direct NDIR CO2; controller reports validity and compensation GY-521 (MPU-6050) Integrated optional sensor I2C 6-axis inertial sensing and interpreted motion Verify mounting, wiring and thresholds for each installation WS2812B RGB LED ring Optional controller-backed output ESP32 data output; typically 5 V LED supply Semantic color and bounded animations via phos-hw v1 Firmware-selected ESP32 pin/count; check power budget and level shifting Servos/motors Planned TBD Future physical movement Not yet specified

docs.title: Face display session
docs.text:
The reference Raspberry Pi face display is part of PHOS while the runtime is running, so its X11 session is configured not to blank or enter DPMS standby at startup. This keeps the fullscreen face visible and avoids HDMI audio being suspended while the display wakes, which can otherwise affect the first local TTS phrase after a long idle period.

For the reference X11 deployment, the desktop-session bridge validates the active local seat0 logind session before importing its graphical environment (including DISPLAY and, where required, XAUTHORITY) into the PHOS user service. SSH/X11 forwarding is not a robot-face display source. PHOS then applies the following idempotent commands:

xset s off
xset -dpms
xset s noblank

Run those commands from the same local graphical session as PHOS when troubleshooting; an SSH shell, including one with DISPLAY=:10.0 or forwarded X11, is not sufficient. See the deployment bridge setup and status checks in installation. If xset is unavailable or a command fails, PHOS logs a warning and continues. The automatic behavior targets the reference X11 deployment. It deliberately skips sessions identified as non-X11; Wayland display-power policy is outside this deployment implementation.

docs.title: BME280
docs.text:
PHOS supports a BME280 through robot.hardware.bme280.BME280Provider and the provider-neutral environmental service. Web Admin → Sensors shows temperature in °C, relative humidity in %, and station pressure in hPa (not sea-level adjusted). Fresh readings can drive the confirmed environmental interpreter; raw values do not reach eyes, LEDs or Vision.

Expected wiring for a 3.3 V-compatible I2C breakout, with the Pi powered off:

Breakout signal Raspberry Pi 3 physical header pin Function 3.3 V-compatible supply input 1 3.3 V GND 6 Ground SDA 3 GPIO2 / SDA1 SCL 5 GPIO3 / SCL1

These are expected signal connections, not a claim about your module's pin order or VIN regulator. Check its schematic/labels before wiring. Pi GPIO uses 3.3 V logic; do not pull SDA/SCL up to 5 V. The bare BME280 supply is 1.71–3.6 V, with VDDIO 1.2–3.6 V; a breakout may add a regulator or level shifter, which must be checked independently. For exposed CSB/SDO, follow the board schematic: CSB high selects I2C; SDO low selects 0x76, high selects 0x77. Do not leave SDO floating or assume the breakout has particular pull-ups. Sources: Bosch datasheet, driver wiring reference.

PHOS uses /dev/i2c-1 and the configured sensors.environmental.i2c_address string, "0x76" or "0x77". It does not scan or silently fall back to another address. The selected adapter checks register 0xD0: BME280 requires chip ID 0x60, BMP280 requires 0x58. A mismatched chip is unavailable; there is no automatic switch to another type. See setup and bus verification. Place the sensor away from Pi/display heat and check readings against a reference; no enclosure-heating correction or calibration offset is applied.

docs.title: BMP280
docs.text:
PHOS also supports BMP280 through robot.hardware.bmp280.BMP280Provider, using exactly the same environmental service and I2C bus ownership as BME280. Select one sensor in Web Admin → Sensors → Type, save and Restart PHOS. BMP280 measures temperature (°C) and station pressure (hPa); it has no humidity sensor. Its reading contains humidity_percent: null; the UI says Not supported, never 0%. Both adapters publish explicit available measurements.

The 3.3 V-compatible I2C wiring assumptions in the BME280 table above apply to BMP280 breakouts too; confirm the actual board schematic and pin labels. Address is configurable as 0x76 or 0x77. Power off before changing modules. Follow the single installation procedure for dependencies, bus enablement and verification.

docs.title: ENS160 and AHT21 through the ESP32 controller
docs.text:
ENS160 and AHT21 share the ESP32 I2C bus. ENS160 uses 0x53 or 0x52; AHT21 uses 0x38. The ESP32 publishes phos-hw v1 sensor_update and sensor_status records over serial, and the Raspberry Pi exposes them as sensors.ens160 and sensors.aht21. Neither device has a direct Raspberry Pi I2C provider.

ENS160 reports estimated eCO2 in ppm, TVOC in ppb and AQI-UBA on a 1–5 scale. Validity and AHT21-compensation status accompany its measurements. AHT21 provides controller-provenance temperature and relative humidity. Per-measurement freshness, validity and controller-session ownership determine usability.

docs.title: Shared I2C bus
docs.text:
BME280/BMP280 and MPU-6050 can share the Raspberry Pi I2C bus if their actual module configuration and addresses are compatible. ENS160 and AHT21 use the ESP32 bus instead.

Wiring and setup checklist:

  • verify the exact I2C addresses of both physical modules;
  • verify module voltage requirements and whether each breakout includes regulation/level shifting;
  • document the Raspberry Pi pins used for SDA, SCL, power, and ground;
  • verify that I2C is enabled on Raspberry Pi OS;
  • distinguish the expected BME280 wiring above from the as-built wiring verified on the real hardware.

docs.title: GY-521 (MPU-6050)
docs.text:
PHOS supports an optional GY-521 module based on the MPU-6050 through robot.hardware.mpu6050.MPU6050Provider, disabled by default. It publishes raw acceleration in m/s² and angular velocity in °/s through the IMU service; it does not publish orientation, gestures or behavior inputs.

The device provides six inertial measurement axes:

  • 3-axis accelerometer: X, Y, Z linear acceleration;
  • 3-axis gyroscope: X, Y, Z angular velocity / rotation rate.

Wire the verified board to Pi bus 1: VCC → 3.3 V, GND → GND, SDA → GPIO2/pin 3, and SCL → GPIO3/pin 5. Use 3.3 V logic and confirm the actual breakout’s regulator and pull-ups before applying power. AD0 low selects 0x68; AD0 high selects 0x69. INT, XDA and XCL are not used by PHOS and stay unconnected.

Important distinction: the MPU-6050 measures acceleration and angular velocity. Absolute orientation is not a direct raw sensor output and would require software-side estimation/filtering if needed later.

The adapter wakes the chip, selects ±2 g / ±250 °/s scale, reads the six raw axes and applies only those fixed scale conversions. It intentionally performs no startup bias calibration because that would require PHOS to be perfectly still. Mounting bias and gravity remain in readings. See installation for I2C verification and setup.

PHOS also derives stable software observations from those raw samples: STILL, MOVING, TILT_LEFT/RIGHT/FORWARD/BACK, SHAKE and IMPACT. They are not hardware interrupts. These observations drive documented eye and LED semantic intent through BehaviorEngine; raw IMU data does not control GPIO, renderer or LEDs directly.

Wiring and setup checklist:

  • verify the exact GY-521 board revision and pin labels;
  • verify its supply and logic-level requirements on the actual breakout board;
  • verify the configured I2C address (commonly dependent on the AD0 pin state);
  • document whether AD0, INT, or other auxiliary pins will be used;
  • verify coexistence with BME280/BMP280 on the shared I2C bus;
  • do not define gesture, orientation, impact, or movement semantics until the corresponding PHOS behavior contract is designed.

docs.title: WS2812B RGB LED ring
docs.text:
The optional WS2812B addressable RGB LED ring connects to the ESP32 controller, which drives its data line and animation timing. The Raspberry Pi sends resolved phos-hw v1 set_led_animation messages over USB/serial; it does not drive the ring's data line.

SemanticLedService arbitrates robot-state, environmental, and temporary user signals. Output requires an active serial connection and LED capability advertised by the controller for that session. Firmware owns the physical data pin, LED count, color-channel ordering, and logical direction/origin mapping.

docs.title: Connection prerequisites
docs.text:
• Enable hardware_controller.enabled in config/phos.yaml.
  • Select the actual hardware_controller.serial.device and baud_rate.
  • Flash phos-esp32 for phos-hw v1 capability discovery, heartbeats, and set_led_animation.
  • Leave the separate legacy led_ring.enabled setting disabled for this build. Its pin/count and per-pixel settings do not configure the ESP32 ring.

See the controller guide and installation steps.

docs.title: Electrical considerations
docs.text:
Power the ring from a regulated supply sized for its specified voltage, LED count, and worst-case brightness. WS2812B rings commonly use 5 V; consult the actual ring's specifications when sizing the supply and wiring.

Connect the ring's data input to the firmware-selected ESP32 output, and connect ESP32 ground to LED-supply ground. Use a suitable 3.3 V-to-5 V data-level shifter where required, plus the manufacturer's recommended data-line protection and supply decoupling. Do not power the ring from a GPIO pin. Keep the Pi connection to the controller on USB/serial.

Start at low brightness. Robot-state and user signals resolve to bounded animations such as solid, breathe, pulse, blink, and spin. On reconnect and a fresh LED capability report, PHOS reapplies the currently resolved intent. Loss of controller connectivity makes LED output unavailable while the display and other robot services continue.

docs.title: Hardware/software boundary
docs.text:
Directly connected hardware does not belong directly inside BehaviorEngine, Vision, LLM, or UI code.

Future integrations should preserve this direction:

Physical sensor / LED hardware
        ↓
Hardware-specific driver/provider
        ↓
Provider-neutral reading or command
        ↓
PHOS core / state / behavior integration

The implemented environmental, air-quality and IMU providers/services are described in architecture. Their typed readings become semantic behavior through the core boundary; other sensors and light-output abstractions remain deferred.

docs.title: Wiring information still to record
docs.text:
The following details must be filled in after verifying the physical components:

  • BME280 exact breakout/module revision;
  • BME280 I2C address on the actual board;
  • ENS160 and AHT21 controller wiring and addresses on the actual board;
  • GY-521 exact breakout/module revision;
  • MPU-6050 I2C address / AD0 configuration;
  • whether the MPU-6050 INT pin will be used;
  • Raspberry Pi SDA/SCL pins used in the final build;
  • sensor power/logic voltage for the exact breakout boards;
  • WS2812B ring LED count;
  • WS2812B external power-supply specification;
  • firmware-selected ESP32 WS2812B data pin;
  • logic-level shifter choice, if required;
  • final connector/wiring scheme;
  • microphone interface;
  • audio output hardware.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• Record new hardware here when it becomes part of PHOS.
  • Distinguish selected/available hardware from software-integrated hardware.
  • Never assume an exact module revision, GPIO pin, I2C address, supply voltage, or protocol detail without verifying the real component.
  • Hardware-specific implementation belongs under src/robot/hardware/ unless the repository architecture explicitly establishes a different location.
  • Application subsystems must not depend directly on Raspberry Pi hardware libraries.
  • Use provider-neutral interfaces between hardware drivers and PHOS core logic.
  • Use mocks/fakes for hardware-dependent tests.
  • Do not make unapproved new sensors influence PHOS behavior.
  • Do not assign unapproved semantic LED colors/states.

docs.title: Current hardware milestone status
docs.text:
Already operational:

  • Raspberry Pi 3 runtime;
  • 800x600 PHOS display/eyes;
  • Raspberry Pi Camera and face tracking.

BME280/BMP280 and controller-backed ENS160/AHT21 integration is implemented; fresh usable readings feed the provider-neutral environmental behavior interpreter. ENS160 eCO2 remains an estimated/equivalent value, not direct NDIR CO2.

MPU-6050 motion behavior and controller-backed WS2812B semantic output are implemented. Follow the sensor mounting and ESP32 ring setup instructions above.

docs.title: How PHOS works
docs.text: PHOS connects physical observations to external agents and turns authorized agent requests into physical expression. The agent decides what the context means for its task; PHOS owns the local runtime and execution.

docs.title: Perceive
docs.text:
Pi adapters and compatible external controllers acquire measurements and observations. PHOS interpreters add confirmation, freshness, and semantic meaning: a temperature measurement and a confirmed environmental condition are different information. Presence describes anonymous human presence, not identity; visible-expression classification does not establish a person's emotions.

The shared physical-context model includes environment, air quality, motion, presence, attention, observed expression, and robot state. Touch gestures are local input with separate REST/Admin telemetry, not a dedicated MCP resource. Raw orientation vectors are available through motion telemetry; MCP physical context exposes interpreted motion rather than those vectors.

docs.title: React
docs.text: An MCP client discovers tools and resources, then reads current context when needed. Clients supporting subscriptions/listen can also receive URI-only notifications for selected semantic changes and read the resource again. This avoids continuous polling for those changes, but is not raw telemetry delivery. The client or host decides whether to invoke agent reasoning.

docs.title: Express
docs.text:
The agent can call tools for supported expressions, temporary thinking visuals, speech, sleep/wake, and user-attention LED signals. Application services check permissions and availability before asking the runtime to act. Local state and behavior arbitration still apply. Optional outputs require their configured hardware and providers.

flowchart TD
  sensors["Sensors and camera"] --> adapters["Pi adapters and Vision"]
  controller["Compatible external controller"] -->|phos-hw v1 serial JSONL| adapters
  adapters --> context["PHOS semantic context"]
  context -->|MCP resources and update cues| client["External MCP client / agent"]
  client -->|MCP tools| services["Identity-bound application services"]
  services -->|Validated requests| behavior["Local runtime and BehaviorEngine"]
  behavior --> face["FaceState and eye renderer"]
  behavior --> voice["TTS and separate playback"]
  behavior -->|Resolved LED intent| controller

Local gaze, blink, and visual behavior are resolved by BehaviorEngine into UI-neutral FaceState; the renderer does not interpret Vision observations. MCP does not expose direct gaze, GPIO, or serial commands. Web Admin, REST, and local voice commands also use shared application services rather than owning separate hardware control logic.

docs.title: Keep the boundaries clear
docs.text:
Boundary Responsibility Physical device / controller Acquire observations and execute supported physical output. phos-hw v1 Carry controller capabilities, validated observations, and resolved LED commands over serial. PHOS runtime Own devices, interpret context, apply state and output arbitration. MCP adapter Expose semantic resources, notifications, and tools through identity and permission checks. External host / agent Choose context, reason about it, coordinate workflows, and request actions.

The runtime is required for both agent-connected and standalone operation. For deeper contracts, read MCP integration, the controller protocol, and the runtime architecture.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
GETTING STARTED

PHOS runs on Raspberry Pi OS with a graphical desktop, Python 3.11+ and the 800×600 display. Raspberry Pi OS Lite alone is not sufficient because the eye renderer needs an active graphical display.

docs.title: Recommended path
docs.text:
1. Clone PHOS and run ./scripts/install-phos.sh as documented in the canonical Raspberry Pi installation procedure.
  2. Test the camera and eye demo before enabling optional Vision features.
  3. Edit the complete canonical config/phos.yaml; its defaults safely start eyes only.
  4. Validate configuration, then start PHOS with the documented foreground command.
  5. Use the documented user systemd service for production startup and browser-initiated PHOS restart.

Web Admin is disabled by default. Enable it in the canonical web section only on a trusted LAN, then complete bootstrap password rotation. Optional expression, environmental, IMU and LED paths each have dependencies and physical checks in the full guide.

No installation commands are repeated here, so the canonical installation reference remains the single source of truth.

docs.title: PHOS installation on Raspberry Pi
docs.text: Current air-quality installation: ENS160 and AHT21 are wired to the ESP32 I2C bus, not Raspberry Pi I2C. ENS160 uses 0x53 or 0x52; AHT21 uses 0x38. Verify supply, logic levels, common ground and serial JSONL telemetry. The controller publishes estimated eCO2, TVOC, AQI-UBA 1–5, ENS160 validity/compensation and AHT21 temperature/humidity. After reconnect, the Pi requires fresh usable telemetry; historic readings are not revived.

docs.title: Reproducible installation from this checkout
docs.text:
Use Raspberry Pi OS with a graphical desktop, Python 3.11+ and an 800×600 HDMI display on the Pi 3. Tk needs an active X display (XWayland on a Wayland desktop). Raspberry Pi OS Lite alone is insufficient. The recommended production launch is the user systemd service below; terminal launch is for diagnostics. These instructions use the desktop user's ~/phos (/home/pi/phos for user pi).

This is a reproducible source/dependency procedure for the checked-out source, not a frozen OS image. cat /etc/os-release, uname -m, python3 --version and apt package versions with your setup notes. See current state and the roadmap for implementation details and planned work.

docs.title: Recommended: unified installer
docs.text:
On the Pi, as the desktop user:

cd ~
git clone https://github.com/phosairobot/phos.git phos
cd ~/phos
./scripts/install-phos.sh

Use an audited commit when one is available. The source checkout already contains config/phos.yaml; do not create an incomplete configuration file. The installer validates Raspberry Pi OS/Debian ARM, installs required APT packages, creates/reuses .venv, installs canonical .[all] runtime extras, prepares the local ONNX model, and performs software-only smoke checks. It does not require connected hardware. OpenCV DNN loads ONNX directly: onnxruntime, TensorFlow and PyTorch are not required.

The APT packages are build-essential, ca-certificates, git, i2c-tools, libcap-dev, opencv-data, python3-dev, python3-opencv, python3-picamera2, python3-pyaudio, python3-smbus, python3-tk, python3-venv, rpicam-apps, and wget. .[all] includes Web Admin/Remote API, Vision, voice (Vosk, Piper, Cartesia, and ElevenLabs integrations), AWS, environmental sensing, IMU, LED-ring, and USB/serial controller Python support.

The optional controller transport uses pyserial (included by .[all]; install .[hardware-controller] for that dependency alone). It is disabled by default; configure a specific serial device path in hardware_controller.serial.device. PHOS does not perform USB-device discovery or poll controller sensors.

docs.title: OpenCV provider invariant
docs.text:
PHOS intentionally uses the Raspberry Pi OS python3-opencv package as its only cv2 provider, inherited by .venv through --system-site-packages. .[all] must not install opencv-python, opencv-python-headless, or an OpenCV contrib wheel: those distributions overwrite the same cv2 namespace and can leave Haar cascades or binary modules mismatched. PHOS uses OpenCV for Haar detection and DNN/ONNX processing, not HighGUI windows; the face display is Tk. The accepted PHOS runtime range is OpenCV >=4.10,<5; it is enforced by the installer smoke check because the Debian package, rather than PyPI metadata, owns that version selection. NumPy remains system/package-manager compatible; PHOS does not pin or downgrade it. Python 3.13 remains supported, with the separate voice extra retaining audioop-lts; voice does not depend on OpenCV.

If an earlier installation ran an affected .[all], recreate the virtual environment rather than uninstalling overlapping files in place:

cd ~/phos
deactivate 2>/dev/null || true
rm -rf .venv
./scripts/install-phos.sh
.venv/bin/python tools/check_opencv.py

The check prints the loaded cv2 path/version and Haar-data path, and fails if multiple known Python OpenCV distributions are visible or the face cascade cannot load.

docs.title: Advanced/manual installation
docs.text:
For contributors or constrained deployments, install the same supported runtime manually:

sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y build-essential ca-certificates git i2c-tools libcap-dev opencv-data python3-dev python3-opencv python3-picamera2 python3-pyaudio python3-smbus python3-tk python3-venv rpicam-apps wget
python3 -m venv --system-site-packages .venv
.venv/bin/python -m pip install --upgrade pip setuptools wheel
.venv/bin/pip install -e '.[all]'

Then prepare the model below and run the installer smoke-check commands. The script remains the recommended path because it performs those steps consistently.

.venv/bin/python -c "import robot; from robot.config import RuntimeConfig; RuntimeConfig.from_file(); print('PHOS configuration ready')"
.venv/bin/pip check

Alternative source transfer: review the destination in run_pi.sh and run it from your development checkout. It copies release scripts, seeds a missing configuration and preserves existing Pi settings/models/administrator data; it neither installs dependencies nor restarts PHOS. Upgrades must merge new required fields from the complete canonical schema. The script has a site-specific destination, not auto-discovery.

docs.title: Camera and display check
docs.text:
Before starting PHOS, run this from the Pi desktop with the camera connected:

rpicam-hello --timeout 5000
.venv/bin/python src/robot/ui/demo.py

Close the camera test before PHOS acquires it. In the eye demo use 1–5 for expressions, arrows for gaze and q to exit. Resolve camera connection/desktop permission problems before proceeding. Camera packages and setup follow Raspberry Pi's supported camera documentation.

docs.title: Configure PHOS and Web Admin
docs.text:
Edit ~/phos/config/phos.yaml. Release defaults start only eyes: tracking, expressions, camera preview, environmental sensors and Web Admin are disabled. Keep this complete file; all required sections (web, display, led_ring, presence, attention, behavior, vision, expression, expression_reactions, voice, tts, sensors, logging) are required, including inactive provider fields and vision.camera_preview. Paths inside the active configuration resolve relative to its directory. YAML uses spaces for indentation; scalar values must retain their intended types. YAML is the sole supported editable format. Migrate a legacy configuration explicitly before startup; PHOS does not read JSON configuration files.

For trusted-LAN administration set web.enabled to true and web.host to the Pi's LAN address or 0.0.0.0; default port is 8080. No provider or password secrets belong in configuration. Validate before any camera/display startup:

cd ~/phos
PYTHONPATH=src .venv/bin/python -c "from robot.config import ConfigRepository; ConfigRepository().load(); print('Configuration valid')"

Enable gaze with vision.face_tracking_enabled: true. Enable the local display picture-in-picture with vision.camera_preview.enabled: true (it is not a web video stream). Keep expressions off until choosing one provider below.

Voice and TTS are disabled by default. The installed .[all] extras provide Local/Vosk STT, Local/Piper TTS, and optional Cartesia/ElevenLabs integrations; models, provider selection, and audio settings remain configuration-driven. Configure cloud credentials only through the write-only Web Admin Credentials page or SecretsService, never in YAML. See voice and TTS for the provider-specific setup and physical-validation limits.

docs.title: Local ONNX expression model
docs.text:
The unified installer downloads and verifies the configured MobileFaceNet model unless the local copy already has the expected checksum. For manual installation, prepare it with:

cd ~/phos
mkdir -p models/expression
wget -O models/expression/facial_expression_recognition_mobilefacenet_2022july.onnx \
  https://media.githubusercontent.com/media/opencv/opencv_zoo/main/models/facial_expression_recognition/facial_expression_recognition_mobilefacenet_2022july.onnx
echo '4f61307602fc089ce20488a31d4e4614e3c9753a7d6c41578c854858b183e1a9  models/expression/facial_expression_recognition_mobilefacenet_2022july.onnx' | sha256sum -c -
wget -O models/expression/opencv-zoo-LICENSE \
  https://raw.githubusercontent.com/opencv/opencv_zoo/main/LICENSE

Stop if the checksum differs. Set expression.enabled: true and expression.provider: "local"; retain the supplied model path, labels and preprocessing. No AWS dependency is needed. The candidate's recognition quality is not established; read model evaluation. Keep neutral reactions disabled until calibrated. Revalidate the active configuration source.

docs.title: Optional NanoDet object-awareness model
docs.text: Object awareness is disabled by default and does not download a model. To enable it, install the OpenCV Zoo NanoDet-m-plus-1.5x_416 FP32 ONNX asset locally, verify SHA-256 4b82da9944b88577175ee23a459dce2e26e6e4be573def65b1055dc2d9720186, and set object_awareness.model_path to that readable file. Set object_awareness.enabled: true only when VisionPipeline is otherwise active; requests require read_perception. See MCP for the model license, on-demand behavior, and error contract.

docs.title: Start PHOS
docs.text:
For a first foreground check from the desktop:

cd ~/phos
PYTHONPATH=src .venv/bin/python -m robot.main --config config/phos.yaml

Check that the startup version matches robot.__version__ and that the logged configuration path is the file you edited. The checked-out commit is tagged 1.9.0; do not treat that mismatch as resolved release metadata. Escape leaves fullscreen; Ctrl+C stops PHOS. Stop this process before installing/starting the production service below.

When web is enabled, open http://<PI-LAN-IP>:8080/, enter phos, set a different 12–256 character password, then log in again. There is no username. Password changes revoke all sessions. Use the administration manual for domain editing, validation, recovery and trusted-LAN HTTP limitations.

docs.title: Managed startup and browser restart
docs.text:
The recommended production launch is deploy/phos.service, a user systemd service running with the desktop user's camera/display/file permissions. No root service, sudo endpoint or adapter-owned shell command is involved. From a terminal in that user's Pi graphical desktop, after stopping any foreground PHOS:

cd ~/phos
mkdir -p ~/.config/systemd/user
cp deploy/phos.service ~/.config/systemd/user/phos.service
mkdir -p ~/.config/autostart
cp deploy/phos-session-env.desktop ~/.config/autostart/phos-session-env.desktop
systemctl --user daemon-reload
systemctl --user enable phos.service
journalctl --user -u phos.service -n 100 --no-pager

The unit uses %h/phos, .venv/bin/python, module execution, and the explicit %h/phos/config/phos.yaml configuration path. Do not install it under /etc/systemd/system or run it as root. The installed desktop autostart bridge validates its own logind session (Active=yes, Remote=no, Seat=seat0, and X11/Wayland) before importing that session's GUI variables and starting PHOS. This binds the face to the physical local display, not an arbitrary user-manager environment. The desktop file assumes the documented /home/pi/phos deployment; for another desktop user, change its Exec path while retaining the same bridge.

Do not run the bridge from SSH. In particular, SSH X11 forwarding can supply DISPLAY=localhost:10.0 (or similar); it is rejected and cannot overwrite the service target. After a local graphical login, confirm the bridge and service:

systemctl --user status phos.service
journalctl --user -u phos.service -n 100 --no-pager

Successful startup logs PHOS DISPLAY: session_type=x11 display=:0 source=local-seat0 (the numeric display is discovered, not hardcoded). A missing local graphical session leaves the service unstarted rather than opening Tk on an SSH display. Direct execution of src/robot/main.py is unsupported because it can shadow standard-library modules.

Operations:

systemctl --user restart phos.service
systemctl --user stop phos.service
systemctl --user start phos.service
journalctl --user -u phos.service -n 100 --no-pager

In Web Admin, System actions → Reload configuration applies logging level, iris theme and every camera-preview setting. Supported Voice & Speech provider and audio-output changes instead use live candidate activation and persistence; other changed fields remain listed as restart-required. Restart PHOS requires confirmation, shuts down the runtime and worker, exits with code 75 and lets systemd start the same entry point after three seconds. Reconnect at the saved host/port and log in again. Disabling web intentionally removes browser access. Manual launches cannot offer browser restart. This never reboots the Pi.

Unexpected runtime or web-worker failure exits nonzero for systemd recovery. The unit limits starts to three per 60 seconds and kills the entire service control group on stop (20-second shutdown deadline). An explicit systemctl stop does not restart it. Fix configuration/dependency/display errors before recovery:

systemctl --user reset-failed phos.service
systemctl --user start phos.service

The service marker PHOS_SERVICE_MANAGED=1 plus systemd's INVOCATION_ID enables browser restart; neither is a normal runtime setting. Do not set the marker in manual launches. See systemd service semantics.

docs.title: Optional AWS expression mode
docs.text:
Camera/OpenCV remain required. The unified installer already includes the optional SDK; confirm its import with:

.venv/bin/python -c "import boto3; print('AWS SDK import OK')"

Configure credentials outside the repository using the standard Boto3 credential chain, preferably the service user's ~/.aws/credentials and ~/.aws/config or a role. Protect credential files with owner-only permissions. The default shared profile needs no shell environment import. The AWS account must allow rekognition:DetectFaces in the selected supported region; no S3 access is needed.

For a named profile already configured for this desktop user:

export AWS_PROFILE=phos
systemctl --user import-environment AWS_PROFILE
systemctl --user restart phos.service

For externally supplied environment credentials, import only the existing names needed by your session before service start/restart:

systemctl --user import-environment AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY AWS_DEFAULT_REGION
# Only when using temporary credentials:
systemctl --user import-environment AWS_SESSION_TOKEN

Do not put secret values in JSON, unit files, shell history or issue logs. The service does not automatically inherit interactive shell variables. Region precedence is expression.aws.region, AWS_REGION, then SDK settings (AWS_DEFAULT_REGION or profile). PHOS does not load a .env file.

Set expression.enabled: true, expression.provider: "aws" and the non-secret expression.aws policy. No ONNX model is required. Restart PHOS. Selected facial crops leave the Pi and are sent to AWS. Import checks and automated tests make no AWS calls. Test live AWS requests only with an authorized account.

Requests are single-flight, cached, rate-limited and backed off on error; they do not silently switch providers. Diagnostics show sanitized latency/request counts. Switching provider or disabling expressions requires restart. See Vision policy.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Missing cv2/picamera2: use the apt packages and the venv created with --system-site-packages; verify imports with .venv/bin/python.
  • Missing image: confirm vision.camera_preview.enabled, the startup config path, and updated Python source; reload/restart. Check phos.log or journal for Camera preview reload failed or Could not render camera preview.
  • Tk startup failure: launch/import DISPLAY and XAUTHORITY from the actual desktop session; SSH alone does not supply display authorization.
  • No faces: check lighting/framing and rpicam-hello with PHOS stopped. Use logging.expression_diagnostics temporarily; restart to apply it.
  • Config save/reload rejection: correct the complete schema and active model/log paths. Save alone never changes the running configuration.
  • No browser after restart: use the newly saved address/port, check the journal and service start limit. Restart invalidates sessions.

Deprecated per-setting CLI overrides are still functional for compatibility; production uses only --config. Supported eye and Vision diagnostic commands remain available; no obsolete provider-specific JSON files are required.

docs.title: Optional environmental sensor
docs.text:
This is an optional PHOS 1.3.0 capability. Leave it disabled until wired according to hardware notes. Confirm the breakout accepts 3.3 V power/logic; the exact board revision is not assumed. With PHOS stopped, on Raspberry Pi OS as the desktop/service user:

sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y i2c-tools
sudo raspi-config nonint do_i2c 0
sudo usermod -aG i2c "$USER"
sudo reboot

Reboot ensures the I2C interface and desktop/user-service group membership take effect. Alternatively enable Interface Options → I2C in sudo raspi-config. See Raspberry Pi configuration documentation. After logging back into the desktop, stop PHOS before probing its bus:

systemctl --user stop phos.service
ls -l /dev/i2c-1
id -nG
i2cdetect -y 1 0x76 0x77
cd ~/phos
.venv/bin/python -m pip install 'RPi.bme280>=0.2.4,<0.3' 'bmp280>=1.0.0,<2' 'smbus2>=0.4,<1'
.venv/bin/python -m pip check
.venv/bin/python -c "import bme280, bmp280, smbus2; print('Environmental driver imports OK')"

For a foreground-only installation, stop the foreground process instead of the systemctl command. The scan should show 76 or 77; -- means no response, while UU means a kernel driver owns that address. Do not force competing access. A responding address alone does not identify the chip: PHOS checks its chip ID against the selected type (BME280 0x60, BMP280 0x58). Keep the bus at its default speed. No sudo is needed for the PHOS process. If access is denied, confirm i2c membership and the device permissions after reboot.

The optional package extra is .[environmental] for both sensors; .[bme280] and .[bmp280] install only the selected driver. Source launch uses the pip dependencies above. RPi.bme280 is a small pure-Python compensation/sampling driver using smbus2, without a CircuitPython/graphics/numerical stack. It is an older library; the adapter is isolated and target-Pi verification is still required.

RPi.bme280 0.2.4 always accesses humidity registers and has no BMP280 sampling API. It is retained for existing BME280 behavior. BMP280 uses the small pure-Python Pimoroni bmp280 1.x driver (with i2cdevice), passed the adapter-owned smbus2.SMBus(1). Its forced-mode update supplies temperature and pressure from one conversion. No CircuitPython, numeric framework or second bus owner is introduced. Only the selected driver is imported.

For an existing config, first merge the required sensors object from the new canonical file as described in migration. In Web Admin → Sensors (or directly in the complete configuration), select type BME280 or BMP280, set enabled to true, choose the detected address, and set polling/stale timing. The canonical defaults are maintained in config/phos.yaml. Save, validate and restart:

cd ~/phos
PYTHONPATH=src .venv/bin/python -c "from robot.config import ConfigRepository; ConfigRepository().load(); print('Configuration valid')"
systemctl --user restart phos.service
journalctl --user -u phos.service -n 100 --no-pager

Manual launch: PYTHONPATH=src .venv/bin/python -m robot.main --config config/phos.yaml. Open Web Admin → Sensors and refresh the page to see current °C, % relative humidity (BME280 only) and hPa, UTC last-update time, age and health. BMP280 humidity is null and shown as Not supported. The active type remains visible when a different saved type is awaiting restart. Save alone changes only the file; Reload leaves all five environmental fields pending for Restart PHOS.

Missing libraries, wrong address, absent hardware, invalid readings or I/O errors make the sensor unavailable without stopping eyes/Vision/web. Retrying starts at the polling interval, doubles to a maximum of 60 seconds (or the configured poll interval if longer), and resets after success. Error warnings are limited to one per minute; measurements are DEBUG-only. Old measurements are hidden immediately after failure or when their age reaches the stale timeout. Last-update/age remain visible. A slow I2C call occupies one worker only; no queue or replacement threads accumulate. Shutdown waits at most one second for that worker; a stuck native call is cleaned up when it returns or by process exit.

Hardware checks: verify the actual address and chip, compare the supported measurements with a reference, check advancing timestamps over several polls, then test a wrong address and recovery after correcting it/restarting. Power off before changing wiring. Confirm eyes, camera and web remain responsive with a missing sensor; confirm disable plus restart removes sensor bus activity. Record actual module, wiring, Pi OS, readings and service logs.

docs.title: Missing BMP280 driver
docs.text:
